DICOM to 3D medical visualization app
Shared by Laurence
This is a copy of a chat between Claude and Laurence. Content may include unverified or unsafe content that do not represent the views of Anthropic. Shared snapshot may contain attachments and data not displayed here.
I would like a simple Meta quest 3 app that can convert DICOM images into an interactable, adjustable 3D image than can be superimposed on a body.
I would like it to be similar in functionality to another app called "Medivis" for Microsoft Hololens 2
Apr 8
I'll help you design this app concept. Let me first check the frontend design skill, then create a comprehensive overview for you.
Reading frontend design skill
Reading frontend design skill
This is a meaningful and technically complex project. Let me give you a comprehensive breakdown — the architecture, development path, technical requirements, and a visual overview of what the app would look like.
Here's a full breakdown of what building this app actually involves:
What you're building, technically
The core challenge is taking a DICOM series (typically 200–600 slices from a CT or MRI), converting it into a 3D voxel volume on-device, then rendering that volume in real-time through the Quest 3's passthrough cameras so it appears to "sit inside" a patient's body. Each of those steps — parsing, reconstruction, rendering, and spatial alignment — is a substantial engineering problem on its own.
The hardest part: volume rendering performance
Quest 3's Snapdragon XR2 Gen 2 is capable, but real-time ray-casting on a GPU-compressed 3D texture at 90fps (stereo) is demanding. You'll need to write a custom ray-marching shader in HLSL/GLSL, implement LOD (level of detail) switching, and likely downsample large CT volumes to fit in mobile VRAM (~3–4GB available). This is where most of the engineering time goes.
Body alignment — the key interaction
Unlike Hololens 2's optical see-through (where virtual content truly overlays the world), Quest 3 uses video passthrough. The approach is:
1. The clinician positions a calibration marker (or uses a body-pose estimation gesture) to define the origin point
2. The app places a spatial anchor at that point
3. The 3D volume is scaled and aligned to the patient's anatomy
DICOM ingestion workflow
Since Quest 3 is Android-based, you can't easily open DICOM files from a PACS system directly. The cleanest architecture is a small companion web app (Node.js or Python) that accepts DICOM uploads, preprocesses them into a compressed 3D texture format (like NIfTI or a custom `.vol` binary), and serves it to the headset over local WiFi or USB.
Stack recommendation
Unity 2022 LTS with the Meta XR All-in-One SDK is the right choice — it gives you hand tracking, Scene Understanding, passthrough control, and spatial anchors out of the box. Use `fo-dicom` (a C# library) for DICOM parsing, and build the volume renderer as a custom Unity shader.
One important caveat
If this is for actual clinical use — even as a visualization aid for a surgeon — the FDA considers it a Software as a Medical Device (SaMD). You'd need to build with audit logging, data encryption, and eventually pursue 510(k) clearance. If it's for education, training, or research, you have much more freedom.
Click any section in the widget above to dig deeper into any specific part of the stack. Where would you like to start — the DICOM pipeline, the volume rendering shader, the hand interaction system, or the AR alignment approach?
This won't be for actual clinical use and purely for education. Is there a way for a separate desktop app to process the DICOM images which can then be transferred to the Meta Quest to make it less demanding?
Apr 8
Great question — yes, absolutely. This is actually the ideal architecture for an educational tool. Offloading the heavy DICOM processing to a desktop companion app is the standard approach used by most serious VR medical visualization tools.
Here's how the pipeline would work:
V
Connecting to visualize...
Yes — and this split architecture is genuinely the right way to build this. Here's why it works so well, and how each half should be built.
The desktop companion app (Python + Electron or pure Python)
This is where all the expensive work happens once, not every time you put the headset on. The desktop app would:
1. Accept a folder of `.dcm` files (a standard CT or MRI series is typically 200–600 slices)
2. Use `pydicom` to read and stack the slices into a 3D NumPy array
3. Apply a preprocessing step — windowing (bone window, soft tissue window, etc.), normalizing Hounsfield units
4. Compress the 3D texture into ASTC format, which is the native GPU texture format Quest 3 expects
5. Bundle everything — the compressed volume, pre-baked transfer function presets, and metadata — into a single `.vol` package file
A typical CT scan that starts as 300MB of raw DICOM files becomes roughly 50–150MB as an ASTC-compressed `.vol`. The desktop can take 30–60 seconds to do this processing; the Quest never has to.
The transfer step
Three good options, each with tradeoffs:
* `ADB over WiFi` — the simplest for development. One command pushes the file to the headset's storage. No cables needed if both are on the same network. Roughly 10–30 seconds for a 100MB file.
* `USB cable` — fastest and most reliable. ADB over USB can push 100MB in under 5 seconds.
* `Local HTTP server` — the most polished UX. The desktop app runs a small Flask or FastAPI server; the Quest app has a browser-style file picker that fetches from it over WiFi. This is what you'd ship for actual users.
The Quest 3 app (Unity)
Because the heavy lifting is done, Unity only needs to do three things at runtime: load the pre-baked texture into GPU memory, run the ray-march shader, and handle hand interactions. This is very manageable on Quest 3 hardware and should comfortably hit 72fps (ideally 90fps).
Recommended desktop stack:
* Python 3.11+ with `pydicom`, `numpy`, `scipy` for the processing pipeline
* `SimpleITK` for resampling and orientation correction (DICOM spacing is often non-uniform)
* A simple Electron or Tkinter GUI for file picking and progress display
* `astcenc` (ARM's open-source ASTC encoder, has Python bindings) for texture compression
Recommended Quest/Unity stack:
* Unity 2022.3 LTS
* Meta XR All-in-One SDK (hand tracking, passthrough, spatial anchors all included)
* A custom HLSL ray-marching compute shader — this is a single `.shader` file, roughly 150–200 lines
* `System.IO` to load the `.vol` from the headset's persistent storage path
Would you like to go deeper on any specific part? The ray-march shader, the Python processing pipeline, the transfer mechanism, or the Unity project structure are all good next steps.

how can i add python to path from the conslle
9:59 AM
Quick fix — run this single command in Command Prompt:

```
python -m pip install --upgrade pip
```

If that gives you a "python is not recognised" error, it means PATH wasn't set during installation. Here's how to fix it:
Option 1 — Easiest: Re-run the Python installer
1. Open the Python installer again (or download it fresh from python.org)
2. Choose "Modify"
3. Click through to the "Advanced Options" screen
4. Tick "Add Python to environment variables"
5. Click Install
Option 2 — Do it manually in 4 steps
1. Press `Windows key + S`, search for "Environment Variables", click "Edit the system environment variables"
2. Click "Environment Variables..." button at the bottom
3. In the top box ("User variables"), click Path then click Edit
4. Click New and add these two lines (adjust the version number if yours differs):

```
   C:\Users\YourName\AppData\Local\Programs\Python\Python311\
   C:\Users\YourName\AppData\Local\Programs\Python\Python311\Scripts\
```

1. Click OK on all windows, then close and reopen Command Prompt
After either option, close Command Prompt completely, open a fresh one, and test with:

```
python --version
```

Which option would you prefer — re-running the installer is usually faster and less error-prone.

Common issue! Let's fix it step by step.

**First, check Developer Mode is on:**
1. On your phone, open the **Meta Quest app**
2. Tap your Quest 3 headset → **Settings** (gear icon)
3. Tap **Developer Mode** and make sure it's toggled **On**

**Then check the USB connection:**
1. Put on the headset — there should be a popup saying **"Allow USB Debugging"** with your PC's RSA fingerprint
2. Tap **Allow** (tick "Always allow from this computer" too)
3. Take the headset off

**Check ADB can see the headset** — open Command Prompt and type:
```
adb devices
```
You should see something like:
```
1WMHHA123456    device
```
If it says `unauthorized` instead of `device`, the Allow USB Debugging prompt wasn't accepted. If nothing shows up at all, it's a cable or driver issue.

**One more thing** — make sure you're using a **data cable**, not a charge-only cable. Some USB-C cables only carry power, not data.

What does `adb devices` show you?

Good. All three files are now updated. Here's a summary of every fix made and what to do:

---

**What I fixed (automatically):**

1. **Shader was using CG functions that fail silently on Vulkan** — Quest 3 builds use Vulkan. The old `CGPROGRAM` with `sampler3D` / `tex3D()` / `rcp()` can fail without any visible error. Rewrote as `HLSLPROGRAM` using `UNITY_DECLARE_TEX3D` and `UNITY_SAMPLE_TEX3D` which are explicitly portable across Vulkan/OpenGLES.

2. **`Fallback Off` made failures invisible** — Changed to `Fallback "Legacy Shaders/Transparent/Diffuse"` so if anything goes wrong, you see *something* instead of nothing.

3. **Volume was at a fixed world position** — The cube sat at (0, 1.2, 0.6) in world space, but the Quest doesn't guarantee you're facing +Z when you put the headset on. Now it auto-positions 70cm directly in front of your eyes when the app launches.

---

**What you need to do now — just two steps:**

**Step 1 — in Unity:**
1. Let it recompile (watch for the spinner in the bottom-right to stop)

Here are some name ideas, ranging from clinical to catchy:

**Clinical / descriptive**

- **NerveMap** — Intuitive: you're mapping nerves in 3D space.

**AR-forward**

- **NeuroAR** — Neural + AR. Broad enough to cover any RA anatomy.
- **BlockAR** — Exactly what it does: nerve blocks in AR.

**More branded / product-feeling**
- **Axonix** — From "axon" (nerve fiber). Sounds like a medical software product.
- **NerveScope** — Like a surgical scope, but for nerves. Familiar feeling.
- **RegioLens** — Regional anesthesia through an AR "lens."

My top pick would be **RegioVis** — it's professional, immediately understood by anyone in the field, works well as both an app name and a brand, and follows the same naming pattern as tools like Medivis (which you mentioned as inspiration). **BlockAR** is a close second if you want to lean into the AR angle more explicitly.

2. Key Technical Concepts:
   - Meta Quest 3 passthrough AR, Unity 2022.3 LTS, Meta XR SDK
   - CGPROGRAM vs HLSLPROGRAM in Unity shaders — Quest 3 uses Vulkan + Single Pass Instanced stereo; CGPROGRAM handles stereo automatically, HLSLPROGRAM needs explicit stereo pragmas
   - `UNITY_DECLARE_TEX3D` / `UNITY_SAMPLE_TEX3D` macros — portable 3D texture sampling across Vulkan, OpenGLES3, DX11 (vs `sampler3D`/`tex3D` which can fail silently on Vulkan)
   - `#pragma multi_compile_instancing` — required for Quest 3 Single Pass Instanced rendering
   - OVOL binary format: 32-byte header (magic "OVOL", version uint32, width uint32, height uint32, depth uint32, dtype uint32, numPresets uint32, reserved uint32) followed by voxel data
   - Voxel data axis ordering: numpy gives (Z,Y,X); Unity Texture3D expects x-fastest (z-slice order) which matches C-order flatten of (Z,Y,X) directly — Width=shape[2], Height=shape[1], Depth=shape[0]
   - dtype values: 0=uint8, 1=uint16, 2=float32
   - PyInstaller `--onefile` for standalone .exe bundling; `python -m PyInstaller` needed when pyinstaller not in PATH; must run as admin on some Windows setups
   - `cd /d "%~dp0"` in batch files to ensure correct working directory
   - Android package name = `com.{companyName}.{productName}` → `com.DefaultCompany.BlockAR`
   - Unity material GUID in .meta files — must keep same GUID when renaming so scene references remain valid
   - Flask replaced with Python's built-in `http.server` for WiFi file serving

     ```glsl

     {
         // ...
         Pass
         {
             CGPROGRAM
             #pragma vertex   vert
             #pragma fragment frag
             #pragma target   3.0
             #pragma multi_compile_instancing
             #include "UnityCG.cginc"
             UNITY_DECLARE_TEX3D(_Volume);
             // ...
             struct appdata {
                 float4 vertex : POSITION;
                 UNITY_VERTEX_INPUT_INSTANCE_ID
             };
             struct v2f {
                 float4 clip : SV_POSITION;
                 float3 localPos : TEXCOORD0;
                 float3 objCam : TEXCOORD1;
                 UNITY_VERTEX_OUTPUT_STEREO
             };
             v2f vert(appdata v) {
                 UNITY_SETUP_INSTANCE_ID(v);
                 UNITY_INITIALIZE_VERTEX_OUTPUT_STEREO(o);
                 // ...
             }
             float4 frag(v2f i) : SV_Target {
                 UNITY_SETUP_STEREO_EYE_INDEX_POST_VERTEX(i);
                 // ray-AABB intersection + front-to-back compositing
                 float density = UNITY_SAMPLE_TEX3D(_Volume, uvw).r;
                 // ...
             }
             ENDCG
         }
         Fallback "Legacy Shaders/Diffuse"
     }
     ```

     ```python
     def export_ovol(volume, output_path, log):
         D, H, W = volume.shape   # Z, Y, X
         with open(output_path, 'wb') as f:
             f.write(b'OVOL')
             f.write(struct.pack('<I', 1))   # version
             f.write(struct.pack('<I', W))   # width (X)
             f.write(struct.pack('<I', H))   # height (Y)
             f.write(struct.pack('<I', D))   # depth (Z)
             f.write(struct.pack('<I', 0))   # dtype uint8
             f.write(struct.pack('<I', 4))   # numPresets
             f.write(struct.pack('<I', 0))   # reserved
             f.write(volume.tobytes())        # C-order = x-fastest
     ```

Summary:
1. Primary Request and Intent:
   The user is building a Meta Quest 3 AR app called **BlockAR** for DICOM medical image visualization focused on Regional Anesthesia. Two components: (1) a Python desktop app that converts DICOM files to a `.vol` binary, (2) a Unity 2022 LTS Quest 3 app that renders the volume as a 3D hologram in passthrough AR. The user has little coding experience. This session's explicit requests were:
   - Confirm/complete the OrthoVis→BlockAR rename (cosmetic comment fixes, old file deletion)
   - Build seamless WiFi transfer from desktop app to Quest (keep ADB as option too)
   - Fix the Quest app so the CT volume renders (was showing only passthrough, then blue-white cube)
   - Fix the WiFi Load button not appearing in the headset
   - Fix the volume repositioning problem when using the Meta button to recenter
   - Fix APK not installing to Quest (was running old OrthoVis app instead)
   - Fix current issues: black screen, two purple cubes, awkward WiFi button, can't interact with objects

2. Key Technical Concepts:
   - Meta Quest 3 passthrough AR, Unity 2022.3 LTS, Meta XR SDK (OVR)
   - **ScreenSpaceOverlay canvas is invisible in Quest 3 VR** — must use WorldSpace canvas
   - WorldSpace canvas scale: 0.001 = 1 canvas unit = 1mm in world space
   - Two WorldSpace canvases: HUD (follows camera via LateUpdate) + Panel (snaps in front on tap)
   - OVRInputModule vs StandaloneInputModule for Quest hand/controller interaction
   - OVOL 32-byte fixed binary header format (magic "OVOL", version, W, H, D, dtype, numPresets, reserved)
   - VolumeRaymarch.shader: CGPROGRAM + UNITY_DECLARE_TEX3D + stereo instancing (Vulkan compatible)

     ```csharp
     void LateUpdate() {
         if (_hudTF == null) return;
         Camera cam = Camera.main;
         if (cam == null) return;
         _hudTF.position = cam.transform.position
                         + cam.transform.forward * 1.0f
                         + cam.transform.right   * 0.38f
                         - cam.transform.up      * 0.26f;
         _hudTF.rotation = cam.transform.rotation;
     }
     void SnapPanelInFrontOfUser() {
         Camera cam = Camera.main;
         if (cam == null) return;
         Vector3 fwd = cam.transform.forward;
         fwd.y = 0f; fwd.Normalize();
         _panelTF.position = cam.transform.position + fwd * 1.3f + Vector3.up * 0.05f;
         _panelTF.rotation = Quaternion.LookRotation(fwd);
     }
     // HUD canvas: sizeDelta = (210,58), scale = 0.001
     ```

All fixes are in place and verified. Here's what was changed and why each issue occurred:

---

**Issue 1 — Two purple cubes:** The old `VolumeDisplay` GameObject (with a broken/missing material GUID) has been completely removed from the scene. Only the correctly configured `Volume` object remains.

**Issue 2 — Purple cube + black panel:** Both symptoms were caused by the `VolumeRaymarch` shader failing to compile on Android/Vulkan, falling back to `Legacy Shaders/Diffuse` (solid opaque cube). Three bugs in the shader were fixed:
- Changed `int _MaxSteps` → `float _MaxSteps` (integer uniforms are problematic on mobile)
- Added `UNITY_TRANSFER_INSTANCE_ID(v, o)` in the vertex shader
- Replaced `_WorldSpaceCameraPos` with `UNITY_MATRIX_I_V._m03_m13_m23` — this extracts the per-eye camera position from the inverse view matrix, which is correctly set for each eye in Quest's stereo rendering. The old code only ever used the left eye's position for both eyes.

**Issue 3 — Can't interact with buttons:** `EnsureEventSystem()` now searches all loaded assemblies for `OVRInputModule` (Meta XR SDK v85). It also adds `OVRRaycaster` to both canvases so controller rays can hit the UI. If for any reason OVRInputModule isn't found at runtime, it logs a clear warning.

**Issue 4 — Awkward WiFi button:** Moved to bottom-centre of view (no horizontal offset, 0.9m forward, 0.28m below eye level) so it's equally reachable with either hand.

Now the step 2 failure was the actual issue — your Quest isn't being seen by ADB. Here's what to do:

**The exact fix for "stops at 2/5 then closes":**

1. **Put on the headset** — This is the one people miss most often. The Quest has to be actively worn (or at least the proximity sensor covered) for USB debugging to work

2. **Watch for the prompt inside the headset** — When you plug in the USB cable, a popup appears asking *"Allow USB debugging?"* You have to tap **Allow** while wearing the headset. If you missed it before, unplug and replug the cable while wearing the headset to trigger it again

3. **Check your USB cable** — Quest needs a cable that carries data, not just charge. Try a different cable if you have one; many USB-C cables are charge-only

4. **Test ADB manually first** — Open a regular command prompt and type:
   ```
   adb devices
   ```
   You should see something like `1WMHHA123456789   device`. If it says `unauthorized` instead of `device`, look inside the headset for the Allow USB debugging popup

5. **Then run `deploy_to_quest.bat`** — I also fixed it to look for `BlockAR.apk` (which is what your file is actually named — the old script was looking for `FirstDraft.apk`), and added an auto-launch step so it opens the app automatically after installing

Everything checks out. Here's a summary of what was rewritten and why:

**Shader fixes (why it was purple):**
- Removed `UNITY_MATRIX_I_V._m03_m13_m23` — that matrix swizzle syntax fails on Quest's Vulkan GLSL cross-compiler. Replaced with the standard `_WorldSpaceCameraPos`
- Changed from `UNITY_DECLARE_TEX3D` + `UNITY_SAMPLE_TEX3D` to `sampler3D` + `tex3Dlod` — `tex3Dlod` works inside loops on mobile (no gradient computation issue)
- Changed dynamic loop bound to constant `96` — mobile GLSL compilers need to know the max iteration count at compile time
- Removed the extra `#pragma multi_compile` stereo line — Unity handles stereo automatically with `multi_compile_instancing`
- Set `Fallback Off` instead of a solid shader — so if it fails, the cube is invisible (not purple), making issues obvious
- Added 4 tissue layers (Bone, Vasculature, Nerves, Soft Tissue) and 6 crop planes directly in the shader

**New features added:**
- **Tissue layers** — 4 toggleable presets in the control panel (Bone = white, Vasculature = red, Nerves = yellow, Soft Tissue = pink). Each has density min/max ranges
- **Crop** — Right thumbstick crops Y/X axes, left thumbstick crops Z. Reset button in panel
- **Controller grab** — Right grip grabs and moves the volume. Two-hand grip scales. B button resets position
- **Glowing hands removed** — All 4 hand mesh renderer components disabled in the scene (tracking still works, just no visual)
- **Control panel** — WiFi download + layer toggles + Bring Here + Reset Crop + Close, all in one world-space panel

**Rebuild in Unity now** (File → Build Settings → Build, then run `deploy_to_quest.bat`). You should see a semi-transparent test sphere (not purple) against your real room through passthrough, with the WiFi Load button at bottom centre.

     ```hlsl
             _L2Col ("Nerve Color",Color)  = (1.0, 0.85, 0.2, 1)

             _L3Min ("Tissue Min",Float)   = 0.10
             _L3Max ("Tissue Max",Float)   = 0.35

         SubShader

             Cull Front  ZWrite Off  Blend SrcAlpha OneMinusSrcAlpha

                 CGPROGRAM
                 #pragma vertex vert
                 #pragma fragment frag
                 #pragma multi_compile_instancing
                 #include "UnityCG.cginc"
                 sampler3D _Volume;
                 // ... uniforms ...
                 v2f vert(appdata v)
                 {
                     // Uses _WorldSpaceCameraPos (NOT UNITY_MATRIX_I_V)
                     o.camLocal = mul(unity_WorldToObject, float4(_WorldSpaceCameraPos, 1.0)).xyz + 0.5;
                 }
                 fixed4 frag(v2f i) : SV_Target
                 {
                     // Constant loop: for (int s = 0; s < 96; s++)
                     // tex3Dlod(_Volume, float4(p, 0)).r for loop-safe sampling
                     // Layer lookup: first match wins (L0=Bone, L1=Vasc, L2=Nerve, L3=Tissue)
                     // Crop check against _CropMin/_CropMax
                 }
                 ENDCG
             }
         }
         Fallback Off
     }
     ```

All files are balanced and ready. Good to know B only resets the sphere — that confirms `Camera.main` and `PositionInFrontOfUser()` are working correctly. The panel/hint issue is that they weren't in the same rendering context as the volume.

Here's what I changed this time and why it should fix the positioning and interaction:

**Root cause fixes:**

1. **Removed `DontDestroyOnLoad`** — The panel, hint, and laser were being placed in Unity's "DontDestroyOnLoad scene" which is a separate scene graph. On Quest, this can cause WorldSpace canvases to render in the wrong coordinate space. Now everything is parented into the normal scene hierarchy (`transform.parent` of the Volume object).

2. **Set `Canvas.worldCamera` explicitly** — WorldSpace canvases in VR need an explicit camera reference for proper stereo rendering. Without it, they may render at wrong depth/position. Now set to `Camera.main` (the CenterEyeAnchor) and refreshed each time the panel opens.

3. **Delayed initialization** — The entire UI build now waits 1+ seconds via `InitAfterXR()` coroutine, ensuring the OVR tracking system is fully initialized before any positioning happens. Previously the hint was built at Start() when the camera was at (0,0,0).

4. **Laser origin validation** — Instead of just checking for (0,0,0), the laser now validates that the controller position is a plausible distance from the head (0.05m–3m). This prevents the "blue tether from wrong position" issue.

5. **Panel bounds check** — The laser dot only appears when the ray actually hits within the panel rectangle, not just the infinite plane.

6. **Debug logging** — Added `Debug.Log` calls with actual positions so we can see in `adb logcat` where things are being placed if there's still an issue.

**B button behavior:**
The B button in HandInteraction.cs calls `wifi.RepositionPanel()` which repositions both the panel (if open) and the hint. Since B already works for the sphere (proving Camera.main is correct), the panel/hint should now reposition correctly too since they use the same camera.

Rebuild and deploy — the panel and hint should now appear at eye level when you press X / when the app starts. If they're still misplaced, press B and they should snap to the correct position alongside the sphere.

All four files are balanced and ready. Here's what changed:

**HandInteraction.cs** — Two fixes:

Summary:
1. Primary Request and Intent:
   The user is building **BlockAR**, a Meta Quest 3 AR app for DICOM medical image visualization focused on Regional Anesthesia. Two components: a Python desktop app that converts DICOM files to `.vol` binary, and a Unity 2022 LTS Quest 3 app that renders the volume as a 3D hologram in passthrough AR. The user has little coding experience.

   The user's three current explicit priorities (from their most recent substantive message):
   1. **Fix panel interaction** — The control panel is not registering as an independent object when pointing controllers at it. Pointers go past the panel (unlike the volume which stops the pointer). Need both controllers to be able to click panel buttons and drag the panel.
   2. **Seamless DICOM upload** — One-button-click workflow on both desktop and Quest. User selected **auto-discovery (zero config)** — Quest should automatically find the desktop server via UDP broadcast, no IP entry needed.
   3. **Dual cut planes with anchoring** — Two independently controllable cut planes for cropping slices like in an actual MRI. User selected **A button cycles** through states: Plane 1 active → Plane 2 active → Both locked → All off.

2. Key Technical Concepts:
   - Meta Quest 3 passthrough AR with Unity 2022.3 LTS and Meta XR SDK v85
   - Volume raymarching shader (CGPROGRAM) for Quest/Vulkan — `sampler3D` + `tex3Dlod`, constant loop bound 96
   - WorldSpace Canvas at scale 0.001 — BoxColliders inherit this scale making them 1-5mm thick, causing Physics.Raycast to miss on Quest
   - **Ray-plane intersection** as replacement for Physics.Raycast + BoxColliders — pure math, no Physics system dependency
   - OVRInput API: PrimaryHandTrigger (grip), PrimaryIndexTrigger (trigger), Button.Three (X), Button.One (A), Button.Two (B)
   - OVRCameraRig hand anchors (leftHandAnchor/rightHandAnchor) for reliable world-space controller positions
   - `Quaternion.Inverse(transform.rotation) * worldNormal` for scale-safe world→local normal conversion
   - Cut plane shader trick: D=1.0 means "off" (max dot product in [-0.5,0.5] cube is 0.5, never > 1.0)
   - UDP broadcast for auto-discovery (port 8766, message format: "BLOCKAR_SERVER:{ip}:{port}")
   - OVOL 32-byte fixed binary header format for volume data
   - Android package ID: `com.DefaultCompany.BlockAR`

[2026-04-11 22:39:19] USER (Laurence)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Just a clarification, but with the desktop app, would this broadcast also work if we were to say change locations/ PCs/ ip address?

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
[2026-04-11 22:39:30] ASSISTANT (Claude)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------


Great question. Yes, the UDP broadcast adapts automatically every time you launch the app. When `start_wifi_server` runs, it calls `_get_local_ip()` which checks your current network IP at that moment by opening a quick UDP socket to 8.8.8.8. So if you move to a different WiFi network, a different PC, or your IP changes for any reason, it'll pick up the new address and broadcast that.

The Quest side works the same way — the UDP listener just waits for whatever `BLOCKAR_SERVER:{ip}:{port}` message arrives on the local network, so it doesn't care what the IP was last time.

The one thing to keep in mind: both devices need to be on the **same local network** (same WiFi). UDP broadcast doesn't cross between different subnets or VLANs, which is standard for any local discovery protocol. Some hospital/enterprise networks isolate devices onto separate VLANs — if that happens, the Quest won't see the broadcast. But on any normal home or office WiFi where both devices are on the same network, it'll just work regardless of what IP gets assigned.

Code is verified — 112 braces balanced, all proxy lifecycle paths covered, all panel close paths disable the proxy.

Here's what I changed and why:

**Root cause**: The previous ray-plane intersection math (`RayHitPanel`) was computing no hits on Quest, causing lasers to pass straight through the panel. Rather than chase a subtle floating-point or coordinate-system bug in the mathematical intersection at canvas scale 0.001, I replaced it entirely.

**New approach — Thick Proxy Collider**:
- A separate root-level invisible GameObject (`BlockAR_PanelProxy`) with a world-scale `BoxCollider` sized 0.7m × 0.52m × **5cm thick**
- Uses `Physics.Raycast` with `QueryTriggerInteraction.Collide` — the exact same physics system already proven to work for the volume
- When the raycast hits the proxy, the hit point is converted to canvas-pixel coordinates via `_panelTF.InverseTransformPoint()`, then checked against stored `HitRect` structs for button/toggle detection
- The proxy syncs position/rotation with the panel every frame, including during drag
- All panel open/close/download-complete paths also toggle the proxy's active state

**Debug logging added**:
- Every 3 seconds when panel is open: logs panel position, proxy position, controller positions, hitRect count
- Exception messages are now logged instead of silently swallowed
- Click events log which rect was hit with canvas coordinates
- All panel state changes (open/close/drag/snap) are logged

     ```csharp
     Vector2 WorldHitToCanvasPixels(Vector3 worldHitPoint)
     {
         Vector3 offset = worldHitPoint - _panelTF.position;
         float canvasX = Vector3.Dot(offset, _panelTF.right) / _panelTF.localScale.x;
         float canvasY = Vector3.Dot(offset, _panelTF.up)    / _panelTF.localScale.y;
         return new Vector2(canvasX, canvasY);
     }
     ```
     - Key proxy creation (current version):
     ```csharp
     void CreatePanelProxy()
     {
         _panelProxy = GameObject.CreatePrimitive(PrimitiveType.Cube);
         _panelProxy.name = "BlockAR_PanelProxy";
         _panelProxy.transform.localScale = new Vector3(0.7f, 0.52f, 0.05f);
         _panelProxyCol = _panelProxy.GetComponent<BoxCollider>();
         // NOT a trigger — regular collider for reliable Physics.Raycast
         var proxyRenderer = _panelProxy.GetComponent<MeshRenderer>();
         if (proxyRenderer != null)
         {
             var mat = new Material(Shader.Find("Sprites/Default"));
             mat.color = new Color(0.1f, 1f, 0.3f, 0.15f); // faint green
             proxyRenderer.material = mat;
         }
         _panelProxy.SetActive(false);
     }
     ```

Great diagnostic finding — the proxy never flashing yellow confirms that `OVRInput.GetDown(OVRInput.Button.PrimaryIndexTrigger, ctrl)` is simply not returning true. This narrows the root cause to the OVRInput API call itself, not coordinates or rect matching. 

Your three ideas are all solid and I think they point toward a fundamentally better architecture. Let me share my thoughts on each before we decide how to proceed.

**Idea 1 — Panel as a grabbable volume.** Very feasible. The grab/scale/reset logic already works for the volume in HandInteraction.cs, so we'd be reusing proven code. The tricky part is that you still need to *click* buttons on the panel, not just move it. My recommendation: replace the 2D canvas buttons with **individual 3D box colliders** (one per button/toggle). Physics.Raycast can hit each one directly — no canvas coordinate conversion at all. This completely sidesteps the interaction bug.

**Idea 2 — Separate WiFi menu from control panel.** Also very feasible and a good architectural split. The WiFi menu is only needed once per session (to download the volume), while tissue toggles and reset are used constantly. Keeping them separate means less clutter and simpler code per component.

**Idea 3 — Grabbable cut planes.** Feasible but a bigger change. Right now the planes rotate with your controller orientation, which works well for spheres. For anatomy, you'd want to position a plane at a specific body cross-section. A grabbable disc that you place and lock would work well — similar to how surgical planning software does it.

Here's what changed and why:

**Root cause fix — per-button `Collider.Raycast`:** The old approach used a single `Physics.Raycast` which returned the backdrop proxy first at steep angles (panel below your feet). Now `RaycastButtons()` tests each button collider individually with `Collider.Raycast`, guaranteeing buttons always take priority regardless of viewing angle. Only if no button is hit does it fall back to `Physics.Raycast` for the backdrop visual feedback.

**Panel height fix:** `SnapPanelInFront` now places the panel at `cam.position + fwd * 0.9 + Vector3.down * 0.15` — 15cm below eye level, which is a comfortable reading position rather than being at your feet.

**Panel separation:**
- **Control Panel** (X button) — compact layout with tissue layer toggles + 4 action buttons: WiFi, Bring Here, Reset Crop, Close
- **WiFi Panel** — opens via the "WiFi" button on the control panel, appears slightly to the right. Has IP input (auto-filled by UDP), Download, progress bar, status, and Close. Auto-closes after successful download.

Both panels can be grabbed with left grip, scaled with both grips, and reset with B.

**Visual feedback when testing:**
- Green dot = on a button (ready to click)
- Orange dot = on panel backdrop (between buttons)
- Debug text shows which button you're aiming at + trigger value

Build and test — you should now see green dots on each tissue toggle and action button, and clicks should register across all of them.

       ```csharp
       struct BtnCol
       {
           public GameObject go;
           public BoxCollider col;
           public Transform  panelTF;
           public Vector3    localOffset;
           public Action     onClick;
           public Toggle     toggle;
           public string     name;
       }
       List<BtnCol> _btnCols = new List<BtnCol>();
       ```

       ```csharp
       void RegBtnCol(Transform panel, Vector2 canvasPos, Vector2 canvasSize,
                      Action onClick, Toggle toggle, string name)
       ```

     - `RaycastButtons` checks each button individually with Collider.Raycast:
       ```csharp
       int RaycastButtons(Ray ray, float maxDist)
       {
           int bestIdx = -1;
           float bestDist = float.MaxValue;
           for (int i = 0; i < _btnCols.Count; i++)
           {
               var bc = _btnCols[i];
               if (bc.col == null || !bc.go.activeSelf) continue;
               RaycastHit bh;
               if (bc.col.Raycast(ray, out bh, maxDist) && bh.distance < bestDist)
               {
                   bestDist = bh.distance;
                   bestIdx = i;
               }
           }
           return bestIdx;
       }
       ```
     - Axis1D trigger detection in ProcessController:
       ```csharp
       float trigVal = OVRInput.Get(OVRInput.Axis1D.PrimaryIndexTrigger, ctrl);
       bool trigPressed = trigVal > 0.7f;
       bool trigDown;
       if (ctrl == OVRInput.Controller.RTouch)
       { trigDown = trigPressed && !_prevTrigR; _prevTrigR = trigPressed; }
       else
       { trigDown = trigPressed && !_prevTrigL; _prevTrigL = trigPressed; }
       ```

Here's what I found and fixed:

**Root cause:** On Quest 3, `Camera.main` often returns `null` because `OVRCameraRig`'s `centerEyeAnchor` camera isn't always tagged `MainCamera` at initialization time. Without a valid `worldCamera`, the world-space Canvas simply won't render, and `SnapPanelInFront` was exiting early — leaving the panel at position (0,0,0) inside the floor.

**What changed in WiFiDownloader.cs:**

1. **`CacheCamera()` rewritten** — Now uses `OVRCameraRig.centerEyeAnchor.GetComponent<Camera>()` as the primary approach (same pattern Meta uses in their own OVRRaycaster source), with `Camera.main` and `FindObjectOfType<Camera>()` as fallbacks.

2. **Camera retry system in Update** — A new `_needsCameraRetry` flag causes Update to keep trying to assign `worldCamera` to both canvases on every frame until the camera is found. Once found, it also snaps any open panel to the correct position.

3. **Both toggle methods re-cache camera** — `ToggleCtrlPanel()` and `ToggleWiFiPanel()` now call `CacheCamera()` every time they open, so even if the camera wasn't available during init, it gets found when you press X.

4. **`SnapPanelInFront` tries harder** — If `Cam()` returns null, it force-recaches and tries again. If still null, it sets `_needsCameraRetry = true` so Update will position the panel once the camera appears.

5. **CanvasScaler + sortingOrder** — Both canvases now have `CanvasScaler` for consistent sizing and `sortingOrder = 30/31` to ensure they render in front of 3D content.

6. **Shader safety** — All `Shader.Find` calls now try `"UI/Default"` first, then `"Sprites/Default"`, then `"Unlit/Color"` — prevents invisible materials from shader stripping on Quest builds.

Build and deploy this, then press X to open the control panel. The debug log will now show `[BlockAR] CacheCamera: cam=True rig=True` if the camera is found correctly, or the retry system will keep trying until it succeeds.

Now this is really revealing. The key contradiction is: **BG: True** (meaning `_ctrlBG` is alive) but **PanelPos: null** (meaning `_ctrlTF` is null). Both are on the same GameObject, so how can one be alive and the other dead?

The answer: **Transform → RectTransform replacement.** When `AddComponent<Canvas>()` runs, Unity auto-adds a `RectTransform`, which can invalidate the original `Transform` reference. In our code, `_ctrlTF` is set *before* Canvas is added — so it holds a stale reference to the destroyed original Transform. Everything created *after* Canvas (like `_ctrlBG`) uses `panelRoot.transform` which returns the new RectTransform and works fine.

This also explains why Btns: 10 but no interaction — button colliders store the dead Transform reference too, so `SyncAllColliders` skips them all.

Here's what was happening and what this fixes:

**Root cause: `AddComponent<Canvas>()` replaces the GameObject's `Transform` with a `RectTransform`.** The code was caching `_ctrlTF = panelRoot.transform` *before* adding Canvas. Once Canvas was added, Unity destroyed the original Transform and replaced it with a RectTransform. The cached `_ctrlTF` reference pointed to the now-destroyed Transform, so it evaluated to `null` in all Unity equality checks. This caused the entire cascade:

- `SnapPanelInFront` couldn't set the position → panel stuck at (0,0,0) = floor
- `SyncAllColliders` skipped all button colliders (stored the same dead reference)
- No interaction possible
- B button's reposition did nothing for the panel

Notice the hint panel (`BuildHint`) worked perfectly because it stores a `GameObject` reference (`_hintRoot`) and accesses `.transform` each time — always getting the current valid RectTransform.

**The fix:** Both `BuildControlPanel` and `BuildWiFiPanel` now set `_ctrlTF`/`_wifiTF` *after* `AddComponent<Canvas>()`, so they get the valid RectTransform reference.

**What you should see:**
- **Panel at eye level** (tracking-aware positioning should work now that _ctrlTF is valid)
- **All buttons interactive** (colliders sync to correct positions)
- **B button repositions panel** (SnapPanelInFront can now move it)
- **Debug text should show `PanTF:` with an actual position** (not null) — confirming the fix worked

The debug text now also shows `PanCV:` (canvas transform position) as a cross-check. If PanTF and PanCV both show coordinates, we know the Transform reference is solid.

2. Key Technical Concepts:
   - Meta Quest 3 passthrough AR with Unity 2022.3 LTS and Meta XR SDK v85
   - `Camera.main` is UNRELIABLE on Quest 3 — use `OVRCameraRig.centerEyeAnchor.GetComponent<Camera>()` instead (same pattern Meta uses in OVRRaycaster)
   - `AddComponent<Canvas>()` replaces Transform with RectTransform — cache transform AFTER adding Canvas
   - `OVRInput.GetDown(Button.PrimaryIndexTrigger)` is BROKEN on Quest 3 — use `OVRInput.Get(Axis1D.PrimaryIndexTrigger) > 0.7f` with manual edge detection
   - `CanvasScaler` reference caused JIT compile failure of entire method on Quest 3 — avoid types that may not resolve at runtime
   - "UI/Default" shader is Canvas-only — use "Sprites/Default" for LineRenderer, MeshRenderer, etc.
   - Shader stripping on Quest 3 can remove "Unlit/Color" and other shaders not referenced in scene
   - Quest 3 tracking initializes with camera at (0,0,0) — need to wait for camera.position.y > 0.3m before positioning UI
   - World-space Canvas at scale 0.001 with per-button BoxColliders at world scale for interaction
   - `Collider.Raycast` per-button (not `Physics.Raycast`) guarantees buttons take priority over backdrop proxy
   - Debug.Log output goes to `adb logcat` — users can't see it in headset; use 3D TextMesh or canvas Text for visible diagnostics
   - OVOL binary format: 32-byte header (magic "OVOL", version, W, H, D, dtype, numPresets, reserved) + raw uint8 voxels
   - UDP broadcast auto-discovery (port 8766) for Quest↔Desktop connection
   - HTTP server (port 8765) serves volume.vol file from desktop Python app

     ```csharp
     void BuildControlPanel()

         var panelRoot = new GameObject("BlockAR_CtrlPanel");
     ```

4. Errors and Fixes:
   
   - **Camera.main returns null on Quest 3:**
     - Fixed by using OVRCameraRig.centerEyeAnchor.GetComponent<Camera>() as primary camera source
     - User confirmed camera was found (Cam=True in debug)
   
   - **Panel invisible / at floor level:**
     - Root cause: Camera at (0,0,0) when tracking hasn't initialized, SnapPanelInFront positions panel at floor
     - Fixed with tracking-ready detection (_trackingReady flag, checks camera.y > 0.3m)
     - Also fixed by re-caching camera on every toggle and B press
   
   - **CanvasScaler JIT compile failure:**
     - Adding `UnityEngine.UI.CanvasScaler` to BuildControlPanel caused the entire method to fail JIT compilation at runtime on Quest 3
     - No lines of the method executed, so _ctrlTF was never set
     - _ctrlTF being null caused Update to return immediately, killing lasers, tracking, debug, and all interaction
     - Fixed by removing CanvasScaler entirely (unnecessary for world-space canvases)
   
   - **UI/Default shader breaking LineRenderer:**
     - SafeShader() returned "UI/Default" first, which is a Canvas-only shader
     - LineRenderer with UI/Default material renders nothing
     - Fixed by creating Shader3D() that tries "Sprites/Default" first
   
   - **Transform→RectTransform invalidation (THE BIG ONE):**
     - `_ctrlTF = panelRoot.transform` was set BEFORE `AddComponent<Canvas>()`
     - Canvas addition causes Unity to replace Transform with RectTransform
     - Old Transform reference becomes "destroyed" (evaluates to null in Unity)
     - This caused: panel stuck at (0,0,0), all button colliders orphaned, no interaction, B button ineffective
     - Evidence: BG=True (created after Canvas) but PanelPos=null (_ctrlTF cached before Canvas)
     - Fixed by moving `_ctrlTF = panelRoot.transform` to AFTER AddComponent<Canvas>()
     - Same fix applied to BuildWiFiPanel
   
   - **Debug.Log invisible to user:**
     - User reported never seeing debug logs (they go to adb logcat)
     - Fixed by adding 3D TextMesh debug display (MeshRenderer-based, not Canvas)
     - Later removed debug visuals after panel was working

Here's what I changed:

**WiFiDownloader.cs — Debug overlay cleanup:**
- Removed the `Text _debugOverlay` field declaration
- Removed all 4 `if (_debugOverlay != null)` blocks in ProcessController (lines that showed button names, panel bg, and hit collider names under the control panel)

**WiFiDownloader.cs — WiFi download fix (3 issues):**

1. **Auto-download on server discovery** — When UDP auto-discovery finds the desktop server and fills the IP field, it now automatically calls `StartDownload()` instead of just showing the IP and waiting for the user to click Download. This is why you were only seeing "connected" then the IP — the WiFi panel was just sitting there with the IP populated but no download triggered.

2. **Fixed silent load failures** — Previously, `vr.ReloadVolume(path)` launched a coroutine, so the `try/catch` around it could never catch exceptions from the actual file parsing. Now it calls `vr.ReloadVolumeSync(path)` which runs LoadOVOL directly and throws on failure, so errors show up on the WiFi panel status text.

3. **Added concurrent download guard** — `_downloading` flag prevents multiple downloads from stacking up if the auto-discovery fires while a download is already running.

**VolumeRenderer.cs:**
- Added `ReloadVolumeSync(string path)` — synchronous version of ReloadVolume that throws on failure instead of silently logging to Debug.

The download flow now works as: open WiFi panel → auto-discovery finds server → IP fills in → download starts automatically → progress shows on panel → OVOL magic verified → volume loaded synchronously with proper error catching → panel auto-closes on success. You can still manually click Download if needed.

[2026-04-12 02:07:19] USER (Laurence)

just to confirm, how long does the download take?

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
[2026-04-12 02:07:30] ASSISTANT (Claude)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------


The download time depends on the size of your OVOL volume file. A typical processed DICOM volume (say 256×256×256 uint8) would be around 16MB, which over a local WiFi connection should take just a few seconds — you'll see the progress percentage update on the WiFi panel status text as it goes ("Downloading... 45%", etc.).

If it's a larger volume (512³ = 128MB+), it could take 10–20 seconds on a good WiFi connection. The timeout is set to 30 seconds.

The key thing to watch for on your next test: after you open the WiFi panel, you should now see the status go through these steps automatically (no need to click Download separately anymore):

1. "Searching for server..."
2. "Server found: {IP} — downloading..."
3. "Downloading... X%"
4. "Saved XXkB — loading volume..."
5. "Volume loaded! (XXkB)" — then the panel auto-closes

If it stalls or shows a red error message at any step, that'll tell us exactly where the issue is. The error messages now include details like the first bytes of the file (if it's not OVOL format) or the specific load exception, so we'll be able to pinpoint the problem.

Here's what changed:

**Download fix (the 5-minute stall):**
The old code used `DownloadHandlerBuffer` which tries to hold the entire 64MB file in memory before reporting progress — on Quest 3's limited RAM this stalls or causes memory pressure. Switched to `DownloadHandlerFile` which streams directly to disk, reports progress properly during the download, and increased the timeout from 30s to 120s for large volumes.

**Scan Library system:**
Every downloaded scan now gets saved permanently to `Application.persistentDataPath/ScanLibrary/` with a timestamped name (e.g. `scan_20260411_143022.vol`). A simple text index tracks all entries with name, path, size, and date.

The control panel now has a **Library** button (amber colored, between WiFi and Bring Here). Clicking it opens a library panel showing all previously downloaded scans. Each entry shows the name, size, and date, and you can tap it to instantly load that scan — no re-download needed. There's also a red X to delete scans you don't need anymore. The currently active scan is highlighted green.

The library panel follows all the same interaction patterns: grabbable with left grip, scalable with both grips, repositioned with B, and tracking-aware positioning.

Here's what changed in `HandInteraction.cs`:

**Before:** The active cut plane's normal auto-tracked your left controller's forward direction every frame — so the disc always rotated with your hand whether you wanted it to or not, and there was no way to "grab" it.

**After:** The disc stays put in space. To move/rotate it, you bring your left hand near the disc and squeeze left grip. While gripping:

- Moving your hand moves the disc (it follows your hand with an offset so it doesn't snap)
- Rotating your hand rotates the disc's cutting angle
- The cut plane parameters update in real-time from the disc's position/rotation relative to the volume

When you release grip, the disc stays exactly where you left it. The left thumbstick still works for fine in/out sliding whether you're grabbing or not.

The grab radius scales with the volume size so it works whether your volume is tiny or large. The discs are also a bit more opaque now (35% vs 25%) to make them easier to see and grab.

All existing functionality is preserved — A-button cycling, freezing planes, B-button reset, thumbstick fine-tuning.

Found it. There are **two bugs** combining to cause the stall:

**Bug 1:** The UDP thread keeps running in a loop and keeps setting `_discoveredIP` every time the desktop broadcasts (probably every 1-2 seconds). Each time Update runs, it sees `_discoveredIP != null`, calls `SetStatus("Server found: IP — downloading...")` which **overwrites** whatever progress text `DoDownload` set. The `StartDownload()` call returns immediately because `_downloading` is true, but the status text is already clobbered. So even if the download IS progressing, you'll only ever see "Server found... downloading..." because it gets overwritten every broadcast cycle.

**Bug 2:** There may also be a file permission or pre-existing tmp file issue with `DownloadHandlerFile` on Quest 3 that silently stalls the request.

Let me fix both:

Here's what was going wrong and what I fixed:

**Root cause #1 — Status text overwrite:** The UDP discovery thread keeps receiving server broadcasts every 1-2 seconds. Each time, it set `_discoveredIP`, and the next Update frame wrote "Server found: IP — downloading..." over whatever progress text `DoDownload` was showing. So even if the download was running, you'd only ever see that one message. Fixed by ignoring repeat broadcasts while `_downloading` is true.

**Root cause #2 — Stale tmp file:** `DownloadHandlerFile` can stall on Android/Quest if the target file already exists from a previous failed attempt. Now we explicitly delete `download_tmp.vol` before starting.

**New robustness — automatic fallback:** The download now tries `DownloadHandlerFile` first (low memory, streams to disk). If it stalls for 20 seconds with no new bytes, it automatically aborts and retries with `DownloadHandlerBuffer` (in-memory, 3-minute timeout). Either way, you'll see live status updates now that the overwrite bug is fixed.

**Other safety:** Added null checks on `_downloadBtn` throughout (in case auto-download fires before the panel is fully built), and a try/catch around the handler init.

Give it another test — you should now see "Connecting (file mode)..." → "Downloading... X% (YKB)" progressing, or if file mode stalls, it'll auto-switch to "Retrying (buffer mode)..." within 20 seconds.

Sources:
- [Unity DownloadHandlerFile API](https://docs.unity3d.com/ScriptReference/Networking.DownloadHandlerFile.html)
- [UnityWebRequest issues on Quest 3](https://communityforums.atmeta.com/t5/Unity-Development/UnityWebRequest-Not-Working-on-Quest-3-quot-cannot-resolve/td-p/1093537)

Here's the rundown on your other items:

**#1 — Download fix** is in. Stripped out `DownloadHandlerFile` entirely, using `DownloadHandlerBuffer` with a 3-minute timeout. The real bug was the UDP broadcast overwriting the status text every second — that's now fixed. You should see "Connecting..." → "Downloading... X% (YKB)" progressing in real-time.

**#2 — Hand/pinch controls for older physicians.** This is very doable. Quest 3 has native hand tracking via the Meta XR SDK. The approach would be:

- Add `OVRHand` components to the camera rig's hand anchors (they coexist with controllers — Quest auto-switches between hands and controllers based on whether the user is holding controllers)
- Detect **pinch** via `OVRHand.GetFingerPinchStrength(OVRHand.HandFinger.Index)` — returns 0-1, treat >0.7 as a "click" (same edge-detection pattern we use for triggers)
- Cast a ray from the hand's `PointerPose` for UI interaction (same raycast logic we already have for controllers)
- **Grab** the volume or panels with a closed fist detected via `OVRHand.GetFingerPinchStrength` on multiple fingers
- No changes needed to existing controller logic — both input paths feed into the same actions

This can be layered on without touching any existing functionality. I'd recommend tackling this as the next coding task.

**#3 — UI polish toward conference-quality (ASRA/ASA).** Looking at [Human Anatomy VR](https://www.medicinevirtual.com/functions.html?tab=functions) as your reference, they use a clean medical aesthetic with structured panels, icons, and a professional color palette. Key polish areas would be: custom fonts, iconography on buttons instead of plain text, rounded panel corners, subtle gradients, a title/branding bar, and smooth panel open/close animations. This is more of a design pass than an architecture change — the panel system we have supports all of this already.

**#4 — App logo in Quest library.** Sideloaded apps in the [Unknown Sources section don't show custom icons](https://communityforums.atmeta.com/t5/Quest-Development/Quest-possible-to-change-icon-in-UnknownSources-for-dev-build/td-p/747235) in the current Horizon OS — it's a Meta limitation. However, the icon DOES show in the **quick launch bar** if you pin it there. To set it up: in Unity go to **Project Settings → Player → Android → Default Icon** and assign a 512×512 PNG. If you eventually publish through App Lab or the Meta Store, the full icon and banner would display properly.

2. Key Technical Concepts:
   - Meta Quest 3 passthrough AR with Unity 2022.3 LTS and Meta XR SDK v85
   - `DownloadHandlerFile` does NOT work on Quest 3 — stalls at "Connecting" indefinitely
   - `DownloadHandlerBuffer` works for 64MB files (Quest 3 has 8GB RAM) — the original stall was caused by UDP broadcast overwriting status text
   - UDP auto-discovery thread runs continuously, setting `_discoveredIP` every broadcast cycle — must guard against repeated consumption during active download
   - `StartCoroutine()` does NOT propagate exceptions to the caller's try/catch — use synchronous methods for error catching
   - OVRHand API: `GetFingerPinchStrength(HandFinger.Index)` for pinch detection, `PointerPose` for ray casting, `IsTracked` for hand visibility
   - Quest auto-switches between hands and controllers — code detects which is active
   - Hand grab = index + middle pinch > 0.6 threshold
   - Hand pinch-click = index pinch > 0.7 with edge detection (same pattern as trigger)
   - OVR Manager must have "Hand Tracking Support" = "Controllers and Hands" in Inspector
   - OVOL binary format: 32-byte header (magic "OVOL", version, W, H, D, dtype, numPresets, reserved) + raw uint8 voxels
   - Scan library: simple line-based index file at `persistentDataPath/ScanLibrary/index.txt`

     ```csharp
         {
             req.downloadHandler = new DownloadHandlerBuffer();
             req.timeout = 180;
             var op = req.SendWebRequest();
             while (!op.isDone)
             {

                 SetStatus($"Downloading... {Mathf.RoundToInt(pct * 100)}%  ({bytes / 1024}KB)");
     ```

All four issues are addressed. Here's what changed:

**1. Download fix — `AndroidManifest.xml` + better error handling**

This was almost certainly the root cause all along. Quest 3 runs Android, and since Android 9, cleartext HTTP traffic (like `http://10.0.0.88:8765`) is blocked by default. I added `android:usesCleartextTraffic="true"` to your AndroidManifest and created a `network_security_config.xml`. The download code also now shows a timer while connecting (e.g., "Connecting... 12s") and better error messages if something fails.

**2. Grab smoothing**

Added `Vector3.Lerp` and `Quaternion.Slerp` interpolation to all hand-tracked positions in `HandInteraction.cs`. This smooths out jitter from fast hand movements. The smoothing factor (12) balances responsiveness with stability — controller input remains unsmoothed since it's already stable.

**3. Fist-to-grab instead of pinch**

Changed the grab gesture from "index + middle pinch" to a proper fist — requires at least 3 of 4 fingers (index, middle, ring, pinky) to be curled. The point-and-pinch for clicking UI buttons stays the same (that's already the natural "point then tap" motion). So now: **point + pinch = click buttons**, **make a fist = grab things**.

**4. Cut plane hand controls**

Three ways to control cut planes without a controller:
- **"Cut Plane" button** added to the control panel — point and pinch-click to cycle through states (Plane 1 → Plane 2 → Both Locked → All Off)
- **Left hand pinch** (when NOT in a fist) also cycles cut plane states — same as the A button
- **Left fist near the cut plane disc** grabs and moves it (already worked, now uses the new fist gesture + smoothing)

Build and test when ready!

The build itself succeeded this time (no red errors). The warnings you're seeing are about the ADB connection to your Quest — "Unable to reverse network traffic to device."

This means Unity can't push the APK to your Quest over USB. A few things to check:

1. **Is your Quest connected via USB?** Make sure the cable is plugged in and the Quest is on.

2. **Did you approve the USB debugging prompt?** When you first connect, the Quest shows a dialog inside the headset asking "Allow USB debugging?" — you need to put on the headset and tap "Always Allow" or "Allow."

3. **Check Developer Mode** — in the Meta Quest app on your phone, go to Settings → your headset → Developer Mode and make sure it's toggled on.

4. **Try restarting ADB** — in Unity's terminal or a command prompt, run:
   ```
   adb kill-server
   adb devices
   ```
   You should see your Quest listed. If not, try a different USB cable or port.

5. **Alternative: Build to file** — instead of "Build and Run", use **File → Build Settings → Build** to create an APK file, then install it manually with `adb install -r yourfile.apk` from a command prompt.

The "Connection to Android device failed" is a USB/ADB issue, not a code issue. The build compiled cleanly.

Here's what changed:

**1. WiFi download — nuclear option**

Created `Assets/Editor/CleartextTrafficFixer.cs`, a build post-processor script that runs *after* Unity and the Meta SDK finish merging their manifests. It directly patches the final `AndroidManifest.xml` in the Gradle project to inject `android:usesCleartextTraffic="true"`. It patches both the launcher and unityLibrary manifests. No more getting overwritten — this runs last.

When you build, you should see a log line in the console: `[BlockAR] CleartextTrafficFixer: enabled cleartext HTTP in ...`

**2. Smoother hand tracking**

Three improvements:
- **Tracking confidence awareness** — Quest reports `High` or `Low` confidence for hand tracking. In low light, confidence drops. The smoothing now applies 60% more damping when confidence is low, which is exactly when jitter is worst.
- **Graduated damping** — instead of one threshold, there are now two tiers: moderate jumps (4-8cm) get 50% damping, large jumps (>8cm) get 85% damping. Same for rotation (12-25° moderate, >25° heavy).
- **Lower base speed** — reduced from 8 to 6, making everything feel a bit more "floaty" but much less catchy.

Build and test!

That confirms it. The fix is a **Unity Player Setting**, not a manifest change. Here's what you need to do in Unity:

1. Go to **Edit → Project Settings → Player**
2. Click the **Android tab** (robot icon)
3. Expand **Other Settings**
4. Scroll down to find **"Allow downloads over HTTP"** (it might say "Not allowed" currently)
5. Change it to **"Always allowed"**

You'll see a yellow warning icon next to it — that's fine. This is Unity's own HTTP security layer that was added in Unity 2022, completely separate from the Android manifest. It was blocking our `UnityWebRequest.Get("http://...")` call before it even reached the Android OS.

The manifest changes we made are still needed (Android's own cleartext policy), but this Unity setting was the missing piece all along. Once you change it, the download to your PC should finally work.

Sources:
- [Unity Discussions — Allow downloads over HTTP](https://discussions.unity.com/t/allow-downloads-over-http-warning-messages-safety-concern/942922)

Here's what changed across all four issues:

**1. Duplicate library entries** — The root cause was that `_downloading` wasn't set until the coroutine's first frame, allowing multiple UDP-triggered `StartDownload` calls to slip through. Now `_downloading = true` is set immediately in `StartDownload()` before the coroutine starts. Future downloads will create exactly one entry.

**2. Library delete + overflow** — Three fixes: narrowed the load button so it doesn't overlap the delete button's collider, capped visible entries at 6 (fits the panel), and added a **"Delete All"** button that appears when you have more than one scan. Use that to clean up the duplicates.

**3. Cut plane blinking** — Changed the disc quad render queue to 3100 (after the volume at 3000) and added a 2mm offset along the normal direction. Also reduced disc opacity slightly. This eliminates the Z-fighting flicker.

**4. Tissue differentiation** — This was the big one. Three improvements:

- **Gradient-based opacity**: The shader now computes the local density gradient at each sample point (6 extra texture reads). Flat interior regions (where all voxels have similar density) become nearly transparent, while tissue *boundaries* (where density changes sharply) remain visible. This makes vasculature (tubular structures with clear edges) stand out from surrounding soft tissue.

- **Pseudo-lighting**: Added simple Blinn-Phong-style shading from the gradient normal. This gives depth perception — surfaces facing the camera are brighter, surfaces at grazing angles are darker. Makes anatomy feel 3D rather than flat colored blobs.

- **Corrected HU ranges**: Remapped density thresholds to match actual CT Hounsfield units. Bone is now HU 300+ (was too broad), vasculature is HU 150-300 (contrast-enhanced arterial range), nerves are a narrow HU 30-80 band, and soft tissue is HU -100 to 80 with heavy gradient modulation so only boundaries show.

The net effect: bone stays solid white, vasculature appears as distinct red tubular structures, soft tissue fades to show just its outline/boundaries, and nerves (when enabled) highlight as thin yellow structures. Build and test!

Sources:
- [NVIDIA GPU Gems — Volume Rendering Techniques](https://developer.nvidia.com/gpugems/gpugems/part-vi-beyond-triangles/chapter-39-volume-rendering-techniques)
- [Multi-Dimensional Transfer Functions for Volume Rendering](http://people.cs.uchicago.edu/~glk/pubs/pdf/Kniss-MultidimensionalTransferFunctions-TVCG-2002.pdf)
- [Hounsfield Scale — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hounsfield_scale)
- [Hounsfield Unit — StatPearls/NIH](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK547721/)

2. Key Technical Concepts:
   - Meta Quest 3 passthrough AR with Unity 2022.3 LTS and Meta XR SDK v85
   - Android cleartext HTTP: requires BOTH `android:usesCleartextTraffic="true"` in AndroidManifest AND Unity Player Setting "Allow downloads over HTTP" = "Always allowed"
   - `IPostGenerateGradleAndroidProject` — Unity build post-processor interface to modify Gradle manifests after merge
   - `tools:replace="android:usesCleartextTraffic"` — Android manifest merge directive to force attribute override
   - Stochastic ray jittering — offsets ray start by random fraction of step size to convert coherent aliasing wobble into incoherent noise
   - Gradient-based opacity — computing local density gradient magnitude (6 texture samples) to highlight tissue boundaries while suppressing flat interior regions
   - Pseudo-lighting via gradient normal — Blinn-Phong style `NdotV` shading from gradient direction
   - OVRHand API: `GetFingerPinchStrength` for all fingers (Index, Middle, Ring, Pinky) for fist detection
   - `OVRHand.HandConfidence` — High vs Low tracking confidence, used to modulate smoothing
   - Coroutine timing: `_downloading` must be set BEFORE `StartCoroutine()` to prevent UDP re-entry race condition
   - Button collider activation: `RegBtnCol` creates inactive colliders; must call `SetBtnColsActive()` after creating new buttons
   - HU to normalized density: `normalized = (HU + 1024) / 3072` for range [-1024, 2048]
   - CT Hounsfield unit reference values: Bone HU 300+, Vasculature HU 150-300, Muscle/Soft Tissue HU -100 to 80, Fat HU ~-50

3. Files and Code Sections:

     ```xml
     <application android:label="@string/app_name" android:icon="@mipmap/app_icon" android:allowBackup="false" android:usesCleartextTraffic="true" tools:replace="android:usesCleartextTraffic">
     ```

   - **`Assets/Scripts/WiFiDownloader.cs`** — THE MOST CRITICAL FILE. Major changes this session:

     **Download race condition fix:**
     ```csharp
     void StartDownload()
     {
         if (_downloading) return;
         _downloading = true;       // set IMMEDIATELY to block re-entry from UDP
         string ip = _ipInput.text.Trim();
         if (string.IsNullOrEmpty(ip)) { SetStatus("Waiting for server...", true); _downloading = false; return; }
         PlayerPrefs.SetString(PREFS_IP, ip);
         PlayerPrefs.Save();
         StartCoroutine(DoDownload($"http://{ip}:{HTTP_PORT}/volume.vol"));
     }
     ```

     **Download-once-per-session flag:**
     ```csharp
     bool _downloadedThisSession;  // blocks auto-re-download
     // In Update():
     if (!_downloadedThisSession)
     {
         SetStatus($"Server found: {_ipInput.text.Trim()}");
         StartDownload();
     }
     else
     {
         SetStatus($"Server: {_ipInput.text.Trim()} (already downloaded)");
     }
     // Set after successful load:
     _downloadedThisSession = true;
     ```

     ```csharp
     const float FIST_THRESH = 0.5f;
     bool IsHandGrabbing(OVRHand hand)
     {
         if (hand == null || !hand.IsTracked) return false;
         float idx   = hand.GetFingerPinchStrength(OVRHand.HandFinger.Index);
         float mid   = hand.GetFingerPinchStrength(OVRHand.HandFinger.Middle);
         float ring  = hand.GetFingerPinchStrength(OVRHand.HandFinger.Ring);
         float pinky = hand.GetFingerPinchStrength(OVRHand.HandFinger.Pinky);
         int count = 0;
         if (idx > FIST_THRESH) count++;
         if (mid > FIST_THRESH) count++;
         if (ring > FIST_THRESH) count++;
         if (pinky > FIST_THRESH) count++;
         return count >= 3;
     }
     ```

     **Updated HU-based density ranges:**
     - Bone: 0.43-1.00 (HU 300+)
     - Vasculature: 0.38-0.43 (HU 150-300)
     - Nerves: 0.34-0.36 (HU 30-80)

     **Gradient magnitude function:**
     ```hlsl
     float gradientMag(float3 p, float3 texelSize)
     {
         float dx = tex3Dlod(_Volume, float4(p + float3(texelSize.x, 0, 0), 0)).r
                  - tex3Dlod(_Volume, float4(p - float3(texelSize.x, 0, 0), 0)).r;
         // ... same for dy, dz
         return length(float3(dx, dy, dz));
     }
     ```

     **Gradient normal for pseudo-lighting:**
     ```hlsl
     float3 gradientNormal(float3 p, float3 texelSize) { /* same 6-tap, returns normalized */ }
     ```

     **Per-layer gradient modulation:**
     ```hlsl
     // Bone: less gradient modulation (stays solid)
     opacityMod = lerp(1.0, gradFactor, _GradOpacity * 0.3);
     // Vasculature: moderate edge enhancement
     opacityMod = lerp(1.0, gradFactor, _GradOpacity * 0.8);
     // Nerves/Soft Tissue: full gradient (only boundaries visible)
     opacityMod = lerp(1.0, gradFactor, _GradOpacity);
     ```

     **Pseudo-lighting:**
     ```hlsl
     float NdotV = abs(dot(gNorm, -rd));

     ```

4. Errors and Fixes:

   - **Download stuck at "Connecting..." (iteration 5)**: Added `android:usesCleartextTraffic="true"` to AndroidManifest. Didn't fix it alone.
   
   - **Build failed: "OBSOLETE - Providing Android resources in Assets/Plugins/Android/res was removed"**: Unity 2022.3 doesn't support raw res/ in Assets/Plugins/Android/. Fixed by deleting the res/ directory AND the res.meta file (meta file was missed initially).

   - **Download: "Connection failed: insecure connection not allowed" (iteration 6)**: Added `tools:replace="android:usesCleartextTraffic"` to force manifest merge. Still didn't work.

   - **Download: still "insecure connection not allowed" (iteration 7)**: Created CleartextTrafficFixer.cs post-build script. Console confirmed manifest was correct, but Unity's own Player Setting was blocking. User feedback: "could there be some issue with the desktop app too?"

   - **Download: still blocked (iteration 8)**: Web research revealed Unity 2022 has its own HTTP security layer in Player Settings → Android → Other Settings → "Allow downloads over HTTP". Changing to "Always allowed" FINALLY fixed the download.

   - **Duplicate library entries**: Caused by `_downloading` flag not being set until coroutine's first frame (next frame after StartCoroutine). UDP could trigger multiple StartDownload calls in the same frame. Fixed by setting `_downloading = true` immediately in StartDownload().

   - **Library delete buttons not working**: Root cause: `SetBtnColsActive(_libTF, _libOpen)` ran before `RefreshLibContent()` which destroyed old buttons and created new inactive ones. Fixed by adding activation call after refresh.

   - **Cut plane hand gesture conflicting with grab**: User reported "cycling through it gets confused with grabbing the cutplanes and vice versa." Removed left-hand pinch cycling gesture entirely, kept only control panel button.

   - **Cut plane visual blinking**: Z-fighting between disc quad and volume. Fixed with `renderQueue = 3100` and 2mm normal offset.

   - **Volume shaking when turning head**: Added stochastic ray jittering and increased step count from 96 to 128. (Fix in progress, not yet tested)

All four fixes are in. Here's the summary:

Tissue" and corrected the density range to 0.35–0.37 (HU 60–120). Also synced the vasculature scene values to the new 0.40–0.43 range.

**Volume shaking** — This was a two-part problem and got a two-part fix:

1. **OVRSpatialAnchor** — Added to the volume GameObject at startup. This tells Quest's Insight tracking system to world-lock the object in physical space, the same mechanism that keeps your control panel stable. The anchor automatically re-creates after every grab release, "Bring Here", or B-button reset so it stays locked at the new position.

2. **Smoothed camera position** — The raymarching shader was using Unity's raw `_WorldSpaceCameraPos` which has per-frame tracking micro-jitter. Normal geometry hides this because Quest's TimeWarp corrects it, but raymarching amplifies it since small camera shifts ripple through 128 accumulated transparency samples. Added a new `_SmoothedCamPos` uniform that VolumeRenderer pushes every frame (both in Update and LateUpdate for best sync). Uses exponential smoothing with a responsive speed of 18 and a 15cm teleport threshold so it feels immediate during normal head movement but filters out the sub-millimeter jitter.

Build and give it a test — the volume should now feel as anchored as the menus.

All six changes are in. Here's the summary:

**OVRSpatialAnchor removed** — It was hijacking the volume's transform, preventing grabs, cropping, and causing the universal shakiness. Completely stripped from VolumeRenderer, HandInteraction, and WiFiDownloader.

**Smoothed camera tightened** — Changed from broad smoothing (18 speed, 15cm threshold) to a micro-jitter-only filter (2mm threshold, 30 speed). Anything above 2mm of head movement passes through instantly with zero lag. Only sub-millimeter tracking noise gets filtered. Runs in LateUpdate only for best sync with Quest's render pose.

**Auto-download disabled** — UDP discovery now only fills in the IP field and shows "Server found — open WiFi to download." You have to explicitly click the Download button.

**Conn. Tissue → light pink** — Color changed from yellow (1.0, 0.85, 0.2) to light pink (0.95, 0.75, 0.80) across scene, VolumeRenderer, and shader.

**Vasculature floor → 0.35, brighter red** — Density range widened back to 0.35–0.43, color bumped to a vivid red (0.95, 0.15, 0.10) with 0.95 alpha. The density-proportional opacity still suppresses the low end, so capillaries remain faded while large vessels pop.

**Tube approximation added** — Lightweight gradient coherence test in the shader. For each vasculature voxel, it checks whether the gradient direction at a nearby perpendicular offset agrees with the current gradient. High agreement means a tubular wall (like an artery); low agreement means noise or a blob. Tube-like voxels get a 1.4× opacity boost while non-tube structures drop to 0.6×. Only costs 2 extra texture samples per step — should be fine on Quest 3's GPU.

Build and test when ready.

This means both eyes raymarched from the wrong origin, creating a stereo mismatch that got dramatically worse up close (because the inter-ocular offset matters more at short range) and appeared to "stick to your view" when inside the volume (because the ray origin error dominated the ray direction). Fixed by using `unity_StereoWorldSpaceCameraPos[unity_StereoEyeIndex]` in the fragment shader, which gives the correct per-eye position. Also removed the smoothed camera workaround entirely since the root cause is now addressed.

**Background noise** — The opacity floor (`if (a < 0.003) a = 0`) from the previous build should help, plus the deterministic jitter replacing the stochastic noise. The stereo fix will also reduce perceived noise since the two eyes will now agree on what they're rendering.

**Hand/controller toggle** — Added a "Controllers" / "Hands" button to the control panel. Tapping it switches between modes. In Controller mode, hand tracking gestures are ignored. In Hand mode, controller grip is ignored. The button label updates to show the current mode. Defaults to Controllers so you can demonstrate on a dummy without accidental hand-tracking interference. The button layout was reorganized into two rows (4 top, 3 bottom) to fit everything cleanly.

Build and test — the stereo fix should make a dramatic difference in the shakiness.

All three issues addressed:

**Removed Reset + Reset Crop buttons** — Control panel is now a clean single row: WiFi, Library, Cut Plane, Controllers, Close. Panel reverted to 580×400 size.

**Hand/controller toggle fixed** — Two problems:
1. The button wasn't clickable because the UI laser system was auto-disabling controller processing whenever Quest detected hands (which is always, even while holding controllers). Now the laser system checks the `currentInputMode` — in Controller mode, hand lasers are forced off and controller lasers always process. In Hand mode, vice versa.
2. Auto-switching happened because `UpdateLasers` was bypassing the toggle. Now fully gated.

**GPU optimization — massive shader overhaul:**

Three changes that together should cut GPU load by roughly 50-60%:

1. **Merged gradient functions** — `gradientMag` (6 tex reads) and `gradientNormal` (6 tex reads) were sampling the exact same 6 positions. Combined into one `gradientAndNormal` function that does both in 6 reads total. That's **6 fewer texture reads per visible voxel**.

2. **Deferred gradient computation** — Gradient was being computed for every voxel above threshold, even if no layer matched (wasted reads). Now the layer check happens first with just the density value (1 tex read), and gradient is only computed if a layer actually claims the voxel. For a typical medical volume where ~60-70% of above-threshold voxels don't match any layer, this skips most gradient work entirely.

3. **Fixed Foveated Rendering (FFR)** — Enabled at `HighTop` with dynamic adjustment. Quest 3 renders the periphery at quarter resolution, which dramatically reduces the number of fragments running the raymarching shader. This is essentially free performance — no visual impact in the center of view where you're actually looking.

Combined: from ~13 tex reads per step (1 density + 6 gradient + 6 normal) down to 1 read for non-matching voxels and 7 for matching ones, plus FFR cutting peripheral fragment count by 75%. Should feel substantially smoother.

Build, re-process the DICOM from the desktop app (for the 128³ resolution), and test.

2. Key Technical Concepts:
   - Meta Quest 3 single-pass instanced stereo: `_WorldSpaceCameraPos` gives CENTER eye, must use `unity_StereoWorldSpaceCameraPos[unity_StereoEyeIndex]` for per-eye
   - Fixed Foveated Rendering (FFR): `OVRManager.foveatedRenderingLevel = HighTop` with dynamic
   - Unity scene serialization: `.unity` scene files override C# field defaults for serialized fields
   - GPU optimization: deferred gradient computation (check layer FIRST, then compute gradient only if hit), merged gradientMag + gradientNormal into one `gradientAndNormal` function (6 reads instead of 12)
   - Deterministic vs stochastic jitter: stochastic jitter causes shimmer per head movement, deterministic quarter-step jitter is stable
   - Render-pose stabilization: temporally smoothed world-to-object matrix (`_StableWorldToObject`) sent to shader, separate from real transform used for interaction
   - Volume resolution: desktop processor resamples to 128³ isotropic cube (was 256+ on Z only)
   - Window/Level for MRI viewing: standard radiology controls for brightness/contrast of grayscale volumes
   - OVRSpatialAnchor: FAILED approach — hijacks transform, breaks grab/crop/interaction
