[2026-04-21 18:21:56] ASSISTANT (Claude)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
All three call sites have the same pattern — they call `PositionInFrontOfUser()` which silently fails if tracking isn't ready. The fix is to make it retry with a coroutine fallback. Let me update `VolumeRenderer.cs`:

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
[2026-04-21 18:21:57] ASSISTANT (Claude)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
[Tool: Read VolumeRenderer.cs]

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
[2026-04-21 18:22:11] ASSISTANT (Claude)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
[Tool: Edit VolumeRenderer.cs]

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
[2026-04-21 18:22:19] ASSISTANT (Claude)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The fix works like this: when `PositionInFrontOfUser()` is called but tracking isn't ready (head at y=0), instead of silently giving up, it now starts a retry coroutine that checks every 0.25 seconds for up to 10 seconds. As soon as head tracking settles (y > 0.3m), it positions the volume and snaps the stabilized pose.

This means if the user loads a volume right after booting the app, the volume will initially appear at the origin but will automatically jump to the correct position in front of them once tracking kicks in — typically within 1-2 seconds.

Build and try it out — the volume should now always end up at chest height in front of you, even if you load it immediately after launching the app.

Here's the step-by-step for uploading to the Meta Quest Developer Dashboard:

**1. Go to the Developer Dashboard**
Head to [developer.oculus.com/manage](https://developer.oculus.com/manage) and log in with your Meta account.

**2. Create your app (if you haven't already)**
Click **Create New App**, select **Meta Quest** as the platform, and name it "RegionalAR."

**3. Upload your APK**
Go to your app → **Releases** → **Release Channels** → pick a channel (use **Alpha** for now). Click **Upload Build** and select your signed release APK.

**4. Fill in Store Listing**
Under your app, go to **Store Listing** and fill in:
- **App Name:** RegionalAR
- **Short Description:** copy from your STORE_LISTING.md (156 chars)
- **Long Description:** copy from STORE_LISTING.md (under 1500 chars)
- **Category:** Education
- **Comfort Rating:** Comfortable

**5. Upload assets**
In the same Store Listing section:
- **App Icon:** download your 1024×1024 from [Canva](https://www.canva.com/d/O5KJ6pzKIkSASD7) (Share → Download → PNG)
- **Hero Image:** download your 4096×1024 from [Canva](https://www.canva.com/d/TQfkdyql3JQsx5l)
- **Cover Art:** download your 3840×2160 from [Canva](https://www.canva.com/d/3rriGF-C6ILXlS4)
- **Screenshots:** the 5 PNGs are already in your BlockAR/Assets/Textures folder (screenshot_01 through screenshot_05)

**6. Privacy Policy**
Paste your hosted URL: `https://<your-github-username>.github.io/<repo-name>/privacy-policy.html`

**7. IARC Rating**
You said this is already done — just confirm it's saved in the dashboard.

**8. Submit for Review**
Once everything is filled in, click **Submit for Review**. Alpha reviews typically take 5–15 business days.

One note: for an alpha/testing release, you can also use the **Release Channel** set to Alpha and add specific test users by email — this skips the full review and lets you distribute immediately to those users. That might be worth doing first so you can get testers on it right away while the full review is pending.

Meta deprecated the web uploader, so you need to use one of their CLI/GUI tools instead. The easiest option is the **Meta Quest Developer Hub (MQDH)** — it's a desktop app with a drag-and-drop interface.

Here's what to do:

**Option A — Meta Quest Developer Hub (easiest)**

1. Download it from [developer.oculus.com/meta-quest-developer-hub](https://developer.oculus.com/meta-quest-developer-hub)
2. Install and log in with your Meta developer account
3. Go to the **App Distribution** section
4. Select your RegionalAR app, pick the **Alpha** channel
5. Drag and drop your signed APK — it handles the upload for you

**Option B — Oculus Platform Utility (command line)**

The dashboard already gave you the exact command. You just need to:

1. Download `ovr-platform-util` from [developer.oculus.com/downloads](https://developer.oculus.com/downloads/package/ovr-platform-util/)
2. Open a terminal and run:

```
./ovr-platform-util upload-quest-build \
  --app-id 26806870765669180 \
  --app-secret d701ed204a0ce91080e01fa1a67bf45e \
  --apk <path-to-your-apk> \
  --channel ALPHA
```

Just replace `<path-to-your-apk>` with the actual path to your signed APK file (wherever Unity saved it when you built it).

I'd recommend **Option A** if you're not a command-line person — it's more visual and also lets you manage test users, see crash reports, etc. Which would you like to go with?

Good. Now to answer your question about the APK name — the APK filename is just whatever you type in the Unity **Build** dialog save prompt. It doesn't affect the app name on the Quest. But if your build dialog is defaulting to "BlockAR.apk", just type "RegionalAR.apk" instead when you save.

The actual app name that shows up on the Quest and in the store is controlled by **Player Settings → Product Name**, which we already changed to "RegionalAR" in your ProjectSettings.asset. You can verify in Unity: **Edit → Project Settings → Player** — the **Product Name** field should say "RegionalAR".

To summarize the three changes just made:

1. **Raised tracking threshold** from 0.3m to 0.6m — prevents the volume from positioning when the Quest reports a partly-initialized head height
2. **Added minimum Y clamp** of 0.7m — even if tracking gives an oddly low head position, the volume will never appear below knee level
3. **Auto-open control panel** on startup — the panel now appears automatically once the app initializes, so users don't have to know to press X/Menu

Here's what changed and why this should fix it:

**The old approach** refused to position the volume if tracking was low, leaving it stuck at the scene origin (y=0, the floor). Even the retry coroutine could fail if tracking took a while to settle.

**The new approach** mirrors how the panels work:
1. **Always position immediately** — if tracking is low, the volume goes to a safe default height of 1.3m (typical seated chest level) instead of being abandoned at the floor
2. **Flag for deferred reposition** — once WiFiDownloader detects tracking is ready (same system that repositions panels), it also calls `RepositionIfNeeded()` on the volume to move it to the accurate head-relative position
3. **`SnapStablePose()` is called inside `PositionInFrontOfUser()`** — this prevents any race where the stable pose gets snapped to the wrong position by a separate call

Rebuild and test — the volume should now always appear at chest level, never at your feet.

3. Files and Code Sections:

   - **`Assets/Scripts/VolumeRenderer.cs`** — Core volume rendering and positioning logic
     - Multiple iterations of `PositionInFrontOfUser()`. Current version (3rd iteration) always positions immediately with a 1.3m fallback if tracking is low:
     ```csharp
     // Track whether current volume position used low-confidence tracking
     bool _needsVolumeReposition;

     public void PositionInFrontOfUser()
     {
         Transform headT = GetHeadTransform();
         if (headT == null)
         {
             Debug.LogWarning("[RegionalAR] PositionInFrontOfUser: no head transform");
             return;
         }

         float headY = headT.position.y;
         bool trackingLow = headY < 0.6f;

         Vector3 fwd = headT.forward; fwd.y = 0; fwd.Normalize();
         if (fwd.sqrMagnitude < 0.01f) fwd = Vector3.forward;

         Vector3 pos;
         if (trackingLow)
         {
             pos = headT.position + fwd * 0.65f;
             pos.y = 1.3f;
             _needsVolumeReposition = true;
             Debug.LogWarning($"[RegionalAR] PositionInFrontOfUser: tracking low (y={headY:F2}), using fallback y=1.3m");
         }
         else
         {
             pos = headT.position + fwd * 0.65f;
             pos.y = headT.position.y - 0.05f;
             pos.y = Mathf.Max(pos.y, 0.7f);
             _needsVolumeReposition = false;
         }

         transform.position = pos;
         transform.rotation = Quaternion.LookRotation(-fwd);
         SnapStablePose();
         Debug.Log($"[RegionalAR] PositionInFrontOfUser: head={headT.position} fwd={fwd} → vol={pos} (lowTracking={trackingLow})");
     }

     public void RepositionIfNeeded()
     {
         if (!_needsVolumeReposition) return;
         Transform headT = GetHeadTransform();
         if (headT == null || headT.position.y < 0.6f) return;

         _needsVolumeReposition = false;
         Vector3 fwd = headT.forward; fwd.y = 0; fwd.Normalize();
         if (fwd.sqrMagnitude < 0.01f) fwd = Vector3.forward;
         Vector3 pos = headT.position + fwd * 0.65f;
         pos.y = Mathf.Max(headT.position.y - 0.05f, 0.7f);
         transform.position = pos;
         transform.rotation = Quaternion.LookRotation(-fwd);
         SnapStablePose();
         Debug.Log($"[RegionalAR] Deferred volume reposition: head={headT.position} → vol={pos}");
     }
     ```
     - `GetHeadTransform()` uses `FindObjectOfType<OVRCameraRig>().centerEyeAnchor`
     - Volume object in scene at position (0, 0, 0.7) with scale (0.3, 0.3, 0.3)

Here's what I found and fixed:

**Root cause confirmed:** Your scene (`RegionalARScene.unity`) had **two conflicting tracking systems** running simultaneously:

1. **XRRig** (Unity's generic XR Origin) — positioned at `(0, 0, -10)` with a "Camera Offset" child at `y=1.36144`, and its own "Main Camera" also tagged `MainCamera`
2. **OVRCameraRig** (Meta's SDK) — with `_trackingOriginType: 2` (Stage mode) and its `CenterEyeAnchor` also tagged `MainCamera`

Having two active tracking rigs and two objects both tagged `MainCamera` was causing `centerEyeAnchor.position.y` to report near-zero values instead of actual head height (~1.6m), which made the volume spawn at your feet.

**What I changed:**

1. **`RegionalARScene.unity`** — Deactivated the XRRig GameObject (`m_IsActive: 0`) and disabled its XROrigin component (`m_Enabled: 0`). This removes the conflict while preserving the object in the hierarchy in case you need it later.

2. **`VolumeRenderer.cs`** — Added debug logging in `GetHeadTransform()` so you can verify in logcat that the OVRCameraRig is being used and reporting correct head height values.

The OVRManager's Stage tracking origin (`_trackingOriginType: 2`) is correct for Quest 3 — it reports actual height above the floor, which is what the positioning code expects.

**Next step:** Rebuild the APK in Unity and test. You should see in the logs something like `GetHeadTransform: using OVRCameraRig.centerEyeAnchor pos=(x, 1.6, z)` instead of near-zero Y values.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
**Found it!** This is the smoking gun. `SpatialAnchorStabilizer` creates an `OVRSpatialAnchor` on the Volume GameObject 1 second after `Start()`. Here's what happens:

1. Volume starts at scene position `(0, 0, 0.7)` — floor level
2. After 1 second, `CreateAnchor()` world-locks the volume to that floor-level position
3. User loads a volume → `PositionInFrontOfUser()` moves it to eye level
4. **But the OVRSpatialAnchor fights back and drags it back to `(0, 0, 0.7)` — at your feet!**

The old code had `ReAnchor()` calls that were removed during the dead code cleanup. Those calls would re-create the spatial anchor at the new position after each reposition. Without them, the anchor keeps pulling the volume back to the floor.

Here's the summary of everything I did:

**Root cause found: `SpatialAnchorStabilizer` was the culprit, not the XRRig.**

During the dead code cleanup, the `ReAnchor()` calls were removed from VolumeRenderer, WiFiDownloader, and HandInteraction. But `SpatialAnchorStabilizer.Start()` still created an `OVRSpatialAnchor` 1 second after startup, world-locking the volume to its scene position `(0, 0, 0.7)` — floor level. Every time `PositionInFrontOfUser()` moved the volume to eye level, the spatial anchor dragged it right back down.

**Changes made:**

1. **`SpatialAnchorStabilizer.cs`** — Removed the auto-anchor creation in `Start()`. Anchors are now only created explicitly after positioning.

2. **`VolumeRenderer.cs`** — Added back `ReAnchor()` (calls `SpatialAnchorStabilizer.CreateAnchor()`) inside `PositionInFrontOfUser()`. Cleaned up all the previous fix attempts: removed the low-tracking fallback logic, `_needsVolumeReposition` flag, `RepositionIfNeeded()`, extra debug logging, and the useless tracking poll loop in `InitAfterXR()`.

3. **`WiFiDownloader.cs`** — Removed the `RepositionIfNeeded()` call that's no longer needed.

4. **`RegionalARScene.unity`** — XRRig stays disabled (no harm keeping it off).

5. **Git repo initialized** with `.gitignore` and initial commit so we can track changes going forward.

Rebuild and test — the volume should now stay exactly where `PositionInFrontOfUser()` places it.

GitHub repos have a 100MB file size limit, and the zip is 345MB because of the bundled exe. You have a couple of options:

**Option 1: GitHub Releases (recommended)** — Upload the zip as a release asset, which supports files up to 2GB. Here's how:

1. Push your repo to GitHub (just the source code, no exe)

3. Tag it (e.g. `v1.0.0-alpha`)
4. Drag and drop the `RegionalAR-Desktop.zip` into the "Attach binaries" area
5. Publish

**Option 2: Split into source repo + release asset** — Commit only the lightweight source files to the repo, then attach the full zip (with exe) to a release. This is the most common pattern for projects with large binaries.

Unfortunately, Canva's API connector doesn't expose the background removal feature — it's only available through their visual editor. But it's very quick to do manually:

1. Go to [canva.com](https://canva.com) and create a new design (2560×1440 custom size)
2. Upload one of the screenshots and drag it onto the canvas
3. Click the image → **Edit image** → **BG Remover** (one click, AI does the rest)
4. The background becomes transparent, leaving just the panel and volume
5. The white canvas behind it gives you the white background
6. Download as PNG
7. Repeat for the other 4 screenshots

It takes about 30 seconds per image. The BG Remover tool is specifically designed for this and handles bone vs. wall separation far better than anything I can do with color thresholds.

Alternatively, if you have PowerPoint, you can do the same thing: insert the image → **Format** → **Remove Background** → adjust selection → save.

Would you like me to help with anything else while you process those?

2. Key Technical Concepts:
   - OVRSpatialAnchor world-locking: Creates a spatial anchor that locks a GameObject's transform to a physical world position. If created at the wrong position, it overrides all subsequent transform changes.
   - SpatialAnchorStabilizer: Custom component that manages OVRSpatialAnchor lifecycle on the Volume GameObject
   - OVRCameraRig vs XROrigin conflict: Two tracking systems in the scene, though this turned out NOT to be the root cause
   - Quest 3 Stage tracking (trackingOriginType=2): Reports actual height above floor
   - StabilizeRenderPose / SnapStablePose: Jitter smoothing system for volume rendering
   - GitHub Pages: Serves README.md by default via Jekyll unless index.html is present or .nojekyll file exists
   - GitHub release assets support files up to 2GB (vs 100MB repo file limit)

     - Fix: Removed auto-anchor creation from Start()
     ```csharp
     void Start()
     {
         // Do NOT create an anchor on startup — the volume starts at scene
         // origin (floor level) and hasn't been positioned yet. An early
         // anchor would world-lock it to the floor, fighting every later
         // PositionInFrontOfUser() call. Instead, the anchor is created
         // explicitly after the volume is loaded and positioned.
     }
     ```

   - **`Assets/Scripts/VolumeRenderer.cs`** — Volume positioning and rendering
     - Simplified PositionInFrontOfUser() back to clean implementation (removed low-tracking fallback, _needsVolumeReposition, RepositionIfNeeded)
     - Added ReAnchor() method called after every reposition
     - Simplified InitAfterXR() to just disable renderer on startup
     - Cleaned up GetHeadTransform() debug logging
     ```csharp
     public void PositionInFrontOfUser()
     {
         Transform headT = GetHeadTransform();
         if (headT == null)
         {
             Debug.LogWarning("[RegionalAR] PositionInFrontOfUser: no head transform");
             return;
         }

         Vector3 fwd = headT.forward; fwd.y = 0; fwd.Normalize();
         if (fwd.sqrMagnitude < 0.01f) fwd = Vector3.forward;

         Vector3 pos = headT.position + fwd * 0.65f;
         pos.y = headT.position.y - 0.05f;
         pos.y = Mathf.Max(pos.y, 0.7f);

         transform.position = pos;
         transform.rotation = Quaternion.LookRotation(-fwd);
         SnapStablePose();
         ReAnchor();
         Debug.Log($"[RegionalAR] PositionInFrontOfUser: head={headT.position} fwd={fwd} → vol={pos}");
     }

     public void ReAnchor()
     {
         var sas = GetComponent<SpatialAnchorStabilizer>();
         if (sas != null) sas.CreateAnchor();
     }
     ```
     ```csharp
     IEnumerator InitAfterXR()
     {
         if (_mr != null) _mr.enabled = false;
         Debug.Log("[RegionalAR] Startup: no volume loaded — waiting for user selection");
         yield break;
     }
     ```
     ```csharp
     Transform GetHeadTransform()
     {
         var rig = FindObjectOfType<OVRCameraRig>();
         if (rig != null && rig.centerEyeAnchor != null)
             return rig.centerEyeAnchor;
         Camera cam = Camera.main ?? FindObjectOfType<Camera>();
         return cam != null ? cam.transform : null;
     }
     ```

1. Open a screenshot in Canva

5. Place the result on a white background

This should take about 1-2 minutes per image since you just need to brush over the rectangular panel area. The BG Remover handles the hard part (separating bone from wall) with AI, and you manually restore the one thing it shouldn't have removed.

That's a good question to think through early, even if you don't flip the switch right away.

My honest take: keeping it free for now is probably the right call. The app is brand new on the store, has no reviews yet, and the Quest medical/education category is niche. A price tag — even a small one — adds friction that could prevent you from building the initial user base and reviews you need for visibility.

That said, RegionalAR does have real value that could justify a price down the line. It's not a toy demo — it processes real DICOM data, has AI segmentation, wireless transfer, multi-tissue visualization. There's nothing quite like it on the Quest store. For context, medical visualization tools on other platforms often charge $10-50+, and even simple Quest utilities charge $5-10.

When the time feels right, a few pricing thoughts:

**$4.99-9.99** feels like the sweet spot for a Quest app like this. Low enough that a med student or curious radiologist won't hesitate, high enough to signal it's a serious tool and not throwaway. Below $5 can actually hurt perceived quality for professional/medical software.

**Free now → paid later** is tricky though. Existing users expect continued free access, and switching can generate negative reviews. A cleaner path might be to keep the current version free with the bundled Head & Neck sample, then offer a "Pro" version (or in-app upgrade if Meta supports it) that unlocks features like AI segmentation support, multiple simultaneous volumes, or advanced visualization modes.

**The real unlock for charging more** ($15-30+) would be institutional interest — if anatomy professors or medical training programs start adopting it. One testimonial from a teaching hospital changes the conversation entirely.

I'd focus on getting 10-20 genuine reviews first. That social proof makes everything else easier.

Here's what the competitive landscape looks like:

**Direct competitors on the Quest Store:**

**Human Anatomy VR** — **$39.99** one-time purchase. 13,000+ anatomical structures, 4.4 stars with 54 reviews. It's an anatomy atlas though, not a patient DICOM viewer. There's also a "Learning" version at **$12.99**.

**3D Organon XR** — Free to download with 2-hour guest trial, then subscription at roughly **$199/year** (~$17/month). Multi-award-winning anatomy atlas with 15,000+ structures, ultrasound sim, multi-user. Again, educational atlas — no patient-specific DICOM import.

**Medicalholodeck** — Free trial on Quest, then subscription (pricing isn't public — enterprise/contact-sales model). This is the closest competitor to RegionalAR: it actually does DICOM viewing and AI segmentation in VR. But it's aimed at institutions, not individual users.

**On Apple Vision Pro:**

**Luxsonic Spatial** — **Free**. DICOM viewer with CT/MRI support in 4K. Consumer-accessible but limited to viewing (no segmentation).

**Falcon Vue** — B2B only, no public pricing. Spatial DICOM viewer.

**XRAIview** — Available on Vision Pro for DICOM viewing. Pricing unclear.

**The key takeaway for RegionalAR:**

You're in a genuinely unique position. The education-only atlas apps (Human Anatomy VR, 3D Organon) charge $13-40 upfront or $200/year, but they don't support patient DICOM data. The apps that *do* support DICOM (Medicalholodeck, Elucis) are enterprise-only with opaque pricing. RegionalAR bridges that gap — real DICOM data with AI segmentation, accessible to individual users on Quest 3.

If you do go paid eventually, **$9.99-14.99** feels like a strong entry point — well below Human Anatomy VR's $40 but signaling it's a serious tool. You could also consider a freemium model: free with the bundled sample volume, paid unlock for DICOM import + AI segmentation.

Good questions — both are important to get right before you flip to paid. Let me tackle them separately.

**Protecting the desktop app**

Right now your GitHub repo is public, so anyone can grab the .exe and source code. A few options in order of complexity:

The simplest approach is to **make the repo private** and only share the desktop app download through a mechanism tied to purchase. You could distribute the .exe via Meta's entitlement system or through a download link that's only revealed inside the Quest app after purchase verification. The Quest app would check the user's entitlement via the Oculus Platform API, and if they've paid, show them a download URL or access code for the desktop companion.

For actual enforcement, you'd want **license key validation** in the desktop app — on launch, it checks a key against a simple server (even a free Firebase or Supabase backend would work). The Quest app generates or reveals the key after confirming purchase. This doesn't need to be bulletproof DRM; it just needs to be enough friction that casual redistribution isn't worth it.

You should also **add a proper license to the repo** (or remove public access). Right now there's no license file, which technically means all rights reserved — but having the source public undermines that in practice.

**On the patent question** — I'm not a lawyer, and patent law is genuinely complex, so please take this as a starting point for your own research rather than legal advice. Let me do a quick search on what's out there.

Here's what I found on both fronts.

**On patents — the reassuring news first:**

I didn't find any patents held by Medicalholodeck specifically. The patents that do exist in the medical AR/VR space are mostly focused on very specific implementations: surgical navigation systems with real-time AR overlays (US9538962B1), dual-mode AR surgical planning workflows (WO2019051080A1), and augmented display systems for imaging labs (US10,412,377). These are about clinical surgical use cases with specific novel methods — not about the general concept of "viewing DICOM data in VR/AR."

The general approach of loading DICOM data, rendering it as a 3D volume, and displaying it in a headset is well-established in academic literature and open-source projects. You can't patent a general concept that's been publicly implemented by many parties. TotalSegmentator (which powers your AI segmentation) is open-source. DICOM parsing is standardized. Volume rendering is decades-old computer graphics.

**That said** — I'm not a lawyer, and a proper freedom-to-operate search requires a patent attorney who can review the specific claims of potentially relevant patents against your exact implementation. If you're planning to charge money, it would be worth a consultation before scaling. Many patent attorneys offer a short initial review for a few hundred dollars, and for a solo developer going commercial it's a reasonable investment.

**On protecting the desktop app, a practical plan:**

1. **Make the GitHub repo private** now — there's no reason for the source + .exe to be public if you're going paid
2. **Add license key validation** to the desktop app. A simple flow: user purchases on Quest → Quest app shows them a unique key → they enter it in the desktop app on first launch → desktop app checks it against a lightweight backend (Firebase, Supabase, or even a simple JSON file on your server)
3. **Use Meta's entitlement API** on the Quest side to verify purchase before revealing the download link or license key
4. **Add a LICENSE file** stating the software is proprietary and redistribution is prohibited

None of this needs to be ironclad DRM — for a niche medical app, it just needs to be enough that someone can't trivially hand the .exe to a friend. The honest truth is that at your scale, piracy isn't the real risk; getting paying customers is.

Sources:
- [Medicalholodeck](https://www.medicalholodeck.com/en/)
- [US9538962B1 - AR in medical environment](https://patents.google.com/patent/US9538962)
- [WO2019051080A1 - Dual mode AR surgical system](https://patents.google.com/patent/WO2019051080A1/en)
- [AR in Healthcare Patent Landscape](https://stg.patent-art.com/knowledge-center/augmented-reality-in-healthcare/)

- [Survey of Medical VR Apps with DICOM](https://www.knowthyself.ualberta.ca/survey-dicom-vrapps/)

Here's a summary of everything that's now in place:

**Done — saved to your BlockAR folder:**

1. **`LICENSE`** — Proprietary license file stating all rights reserved, redistribution prohibited, and requiring a valid license key for use.

- **Make the GitHub repo private** — Settings → Danger Zone → Change visibility → Private.

The system is intentionally simple (no server, no internet required) which fits your app well — medical professionals in hospital networks often have restricted internet access, so offline validation is actually a feature.

     ```python
     _SECRET = b"6n09hzVNsk4N44K431AJp5dOs-ciY7RHcACQzre3KMswwMdPBIO118vyOI528H-L"
     _MASTER_KEY = "RGNL-1D92-1B9C-8C9D-614E"
     
     def generate_key(user_seed: str) -> str:
         user_seed = user_seed.strip().lower()
         mac = hmac.new(_SECRET, user_seed.encode('utf-8'), hashlib.sha256)
         hex_digest = mac.hexdigest()[:16].upper()
         return f"RGNL-{hex_digest[:4]}-{hex_digest[4:8]}-{hex_digest[8:12]}-{hex_digest[12:16]}"
     
     def validate_key(user_seed: str, key: str) -> bool:
         key = key.strip().upper()
         if key == _MASTER_KEY:
             return True
         expected = generate_key(user_seed)
         return hmac.compare_digest(key, expected)
     ```

     if __name__ == "__main__":

   - **`Assets/Scripts/LicenseKeyGenerator.cs`**
     - Unity/C# script for Quest-side key generation
     - Uses same HMAC-SHA256 secret as Python side
     - Static methods: `GenerateKey(string userSeed)` and `ValidateKey(string userSeed, string key)`
     ```csharp
     private const string SECRET = "6n09hzVNsk4N44K431AJp5dOs-ciY7RHcACQzre3KMswwMdPBIO118vyOI528H-L";
     
     public static string GenerateKey(string userSeed)
     {
         userSeed = userSeed.Trim().ToLowerInvariant();
         byte[] secretBytes = Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes(SECRET);
         byte[] seedBytes = Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes(userSeed);
         using (var hmac = new HMACSHA256(secretBytes))
         {
             byte[] hash = hmac.ComputeHash(seedBytes);
             string hex = BitConverter.ToString(hash, 0, 8).Replace("-", "").ToUpperInvariant();
             return $"RGNL-{hex.Substring(0, 4)}-{hex.Substring(4, 4)}-{hex.Substring(8, 4)}-{hex.Substring(12, 4)}";
         }
     }
     ```

Yes, with the current code the desktop app will check for a valid license every time it launches. But it only shows the activation dialog the **first time** (or if the license file gets deleted). Here's the flow:

1. **First launch** — no `.regionalar_license` file exists, so the dialog pops up asking for username + key

So in practice, users activate once and never see the dialog again. You can also use the master key (`RGNL-1D92-1B9C-8C9D-614E`) with any username to unlock it for testing or support purposes.

[2026-04-23 19:52:29] USER (Laurence)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
so for customers, they can put any username they want for log in?

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
[2026-04-23 19:52:40] ASSISTANT (Claude)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Good question — no, for real customers the username matters. Here's how it would work:

The Quest app generates a key tied to a **specific** username (their Oculus username or a code the app shows them). So the customer needs to enter the **exact same username** that the Quest app used when generating their key. If the username doesn't match, the HMAC produces a different key and validation fails.

The flow for a customer would be:

1. They buy RegionalAR on the Quest Store
2. In the Quest app, they go to Settings → Desktop License
3. The app shows them their username and generated key
4. They type both into the desktop app's activation dialog — they have to match exactly

The master key is the only one that skips the username check, and only you have that. So you wouldn't share it with customers.

That said, the Quest-side UI for showing the license key doesn't exist yet — you'd need to add a button/screen in the Quest app that calls `LicenseKeyGenerator.GenerateKey()` with the user's seed and displays the result. That's the last piece to wire up when you're ready to go paid.

awesome, how can I go about monetizing it such that the quest app itself is free, but accessing the desktop app requires payment?

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
[2026-04-23 20:01:53] ASSISTANT (Claude)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Great question. Since the Quest app is already on the Meta Store and the license system is built in, you have a few solid options:

**Meta Quest Store In-App Purchase (recommended)** — This is the most seamless approach. You'd make the Quest app free to download, then add an IAP (in-app purchase) for the "Desktop License" unlock. After the user completes the purchase, the LICENSE button on the control panel becomes active and shows their key. Before purchase, tapping LICENSE would show a prompt like "Unlock Desktop App — $9.99" that triggers the Meta payment flow. This keeps everything in one ecosystem — users pay through the same store they downloaded from, and Meta handles all the payment processing. You'd use the Oculus Platform SDK's IAP API to check purchase status and gate the LICENSE panel accordingly.

**Gumroad / Lemonsqueezy / Stripe** — If you'd rather avoid Meta's 30% cut, you could sell license keys directly through a simple storefront. You'd generate keys in bulk using `python license_manager.py generate <seed>` and deliver them via email after purchase. The downside is it's more manual, and you'd need to manage the key-to-customer mapping yourself.

**Itch.io** — You could list the desktop app as a paid download on itch.io. Users would get the exe plus a license key. Itch.io takes a much smaller cut (you choose, even 0%). But it separates the purchase from the Quest app experience.

The Meta IAP route is the cleanest user experience by far. Want me to wire up the IAP gating so the LICENSE panel only opens after purchase? I'd need to add the Oculus Platform SDK entitlement check — it's a few lines in `WiFiDownloader.cs` to check if the user owns the "desktop_license" IAP product before showing the key.

Everything's in place. Here's a summary of what's been implemented and what you need to do on the Meta Developer Dashboard side:

**What the code does now:**

- On app launch, it initializes the Meta Platform SDK and checks if the user has purchased the `desktop_license` IAP
- When the user taps **LICENSE** on the control panel:
  - **If not purchased** → shows a purchase prompt with description, $9.99 price, and a PURCHASE button that triggers Meta's checkout flow
  - **If purchased** → shows the code + license key for activating the desktop app
- After a successful purchase, it automatically rebuilds the panel to show the key

**What you need to do in the Meta Developer Dashboard:**

1. Go to your app's page at [developer.oculus.com](https://developer.oculus.com)
2. Set the **App ID** — copy it into Unity under `Meta > Platform > Edit Settings > Oculus Mobile App ID`
3. Navigate to **Platform Services > In-App Purchases**
4. Create a new **Durable** IAP item (not consumable — they buy it once):
   - **SKU:** `desktop_license` (must match exactly)
   - **Name:** Desktop License
   - **Price:** $9.99
   - **Description:** Unlock the RegionalAR Desktop companion app for DICOM import and AI segmentation
5. Submit the IAP for review

The app itself stays free on the Quest Store — the IAP is the only paid part. Ready to push through GitHub Desktop?

**For the Meta IAP payment** — the code is already wired up to call `IAP.LaunchCheckoutFlow("desktop_license")` when PURCHASE is tapped. But for it to actually work, you need to set up the IAP product in the Meta Developer Dashboard:

1. Go to [developer.oculus.com](https://developer.oculus.com) → your RegionalAR app
2. Copy your **App ID** from the dashboard
3. In Unity: go to **Meta > Platform > Edit Settings** and paste the App ID into the **Oculus Mobile App ID** field
4. In the dashboard, go to **Platform Services > In-App Purchases**
5. Click **Create IAP Item**:
   - **Type:** Durable (one-time purchase, not consumable)
   - **SKU:** `desktop_license` (must be exactly this — it matches the code)
   - **Name:** Desktop License
   - **Price:** $9.99
   - **Description:** Unlock the RegionalAR Desktop companion app for DICOM import and AI segmentation
6. Submit the IAP for review

Until the App ID is set and the IAP product is created in the dashboard, the PURCHASE button won't do anything (it'll log an error in the Quest logs). Once both are configured, tapping PURCHASE will bring up Meta's native payment overlay — the same one users see when buying any Quest app or add-on.

[2026-04-24 18:36:19] ASSISTANT (Claude)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
All four mesh loaders are now fixed. Here's what changed and why:

**The bug:** `SetMeshEnabled(false)` in `VolumeRenderer.TryLoadCompanionMesh()` only called `_meshGO.SetActive(false)` — hiding the old mesh but leaving the mesh data in memory. When a new volume had no companion mesh file (e.g., left leg with no `.omsh`), `TryLoadCompanion` returned `false` early without touching the old `_mesh`. Since `HasMesh` was still `true` from the old data, any UI toggle could re-show the stale Head & Neck mesh.

**The fix:** Each loader's `TryLoadCompanion` now **destroys the old mesh and nulls it out** at the very start, before even checking if the new file exists. This means:

- If the new file exists → old mesh is destroyed, new mesh loads in its place
- If the new file is missing → old mesh is destroyed, `HasMesh` returns `false`, nothing can be toggled back on

Push via GitHub Desktop, rebuild the Quest app, and test with the left leg again. The old Head & Neck meshes should be completely gone this time.

just realized that this one can't detect a GPU since I'm using an AMD gpu. Is there a way to run it through AMD's 7900xt?

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
[2026-04-24 19:54:22] ASSISTANT (Claude)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Unfortunately this is a tricky situation. TotalSegmentator uses PyTorch with nnU-Net, which is built around CUDA (NVIDIA only). For AMD GPUs on Windows, the options are limited:

**DirectML (best bet for Windows + AMD):**
```
pip install torch-directml
```
This adds a `"dml"` device to PyTorch that works with AMD GPUs. However, TotalSegmentator and nnU-Net call `torch.cuda` internally, so they won't automatically use it — the code would need modifications to route computations to the DirectML device, and not all PyTorch operations are supported yet. It's hit-or-miss with complex models like nnU-Net.

**ROCm (AMD's CUDA equivalent):**
AMD's official ML stack, but it's Linux-only. No Windows support for the 7900 XT.

**The practical reality:**
TotalSegmentator on Windows with AMD is effectively CPU-only right now. The processing will still work — just slower (maybe 5-10 minutes per scan instead of 1-2 minutes on an NVIDIA GPU). The desktop app already handles this gracefully by falling back to CPU when no CUDA device is found.

If GPU acceleration matters a lot for your workflow, the two realistic paths would be either dual-booting Linux with ROCm, or picking up a used NVIDIA card for processing. But for occasional scans, CPU mode works fine — it's just a longer wait.

Want me to look into whether DirectML can be wired into the processing pipeline, or is CPU speed acceptable for now?

The fix is in. Here's what it does:

**Bone preservation:** When the resampled volume has any axis smaller than 96 voxels (like the 38×49 in your left leg), it boosts all bone voxels (HU > 700) to HU 2048 before resampling. This way, even after linear interpolation averages bone with surrounding soft tissue, the result stays above the bone rendering threshold. For example, a 3mm cortical bone wall in a 3.66mm voxel: 0.82 × 2048 + 0.18 × 50 = HU 1688 → density 0.883, well above the 0.561 threshold.

**Lower mesh minimum:** Reduced the bone mesh skip threshold from 5000 to 2000 voxels, so it's less likely to skip mesh generation for smaller or elongated volumes.

To your question about 3D Slicer — Slicer uses a completely different rendering pipeline (GPU-based volume rendering with adaptive sampling and much higher step counts), which is why your reference image looks great. The issue isn't really about interpretation of the data, it's about preserving bone detail during the aggressive downsampling needed to fit the Quest 3's GPU budget.

Reprocess the left leg NRRD with the updated desktop app and you should see solid bones this time. No Quest rebuild needed — this is a desktop-side fix only.

[2026-04-24 20:45:19] ASSISTANT (Claude)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
It's not an NRRD limitation — the same problem would happen with DICOM files of this scan. The core issue is the **extreme aspect ratio**: your leg scan is 937mm long × 137mm wide. To fit the Quest's 256³ texture, it gets crushed from 195×257 down to **38×49 voxels in XY**. At that resolution, the entire femur cross-section is maybe 2 voxels wide. No amount of boosting can recreate detail that's been lost to a 5:1 downsampling.

There are a few ways to improve this substantially. The quickest win: instead of boosting and then linear-resampling (which still averages bone away), I'll **resample the bone mask separately with nearest-neighbor** so bone locations survive perfectly, then stamp them into the volume:

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
[2026-04-24 20:45:23] ASSISTANT (Claude)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
[Tool: Read dicom_processor.py]

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
[2026-04-24 20:45:45] ASSISTANT (Claude)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
[Tool: Edit dicom_processor.py]

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
[2026-04-24 20:45:59] ASSISTANT (Claude)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
This new approach should be significantly better:

1. **Creates a bone mask** (HU > 300) from the full-resolution volume
2. **Dilates it slightly** in XY so thin cortical walls don't fall between output voxels
3. **Resamples the mask with nearest-neighbor** (no averaging — a voxel is either bone or not)
4. **Resamples the volume with linear** (keeps soft tissue smooth)
5. **Stamps bone into the resampled volume** at max HU wherever the NN mask says bone exists

To your question about DICOM files — **yes, absolutely.** The issue isn't the file format (NRRD vs DICOM), it's the **aspect ratio** of the scan. Your left leg NRRD is 195×257×3000 voxels — that 3000-slice Z axis is what causes the extreme downsampling. A typical abdominal or head CT with 300-500 slices at 512×512 would resample to roughly 200×200×256, which gives MUCH better XY resolution. The Head & Neck CTA works so well because it has a more balanced aspect ratio.

So a shorter DICOM scan covering just the knee or thigh (300-500 slices) would look dramatically better than this full-leg 3000-slice NRRD. Try it and you'll see a big difference.

In the meantime, reprocess the left leg with this updated code — the NN resample + dilation should give you the best result possible at 38×49 resolution.

Done. The tissue preservation now handles all three types:

- **Bone** (HU > 300) → stamped at HU 2048 → renders in bone layer (white/cream)
- **Vasculature** (HU 150-300) → stamped at HU 275 → renders in vasculature layer (red)
- **Nerves** (HU 110-150) → stamped at HU 140 → renders in nerve layer (yellow)

The masks are mutually exclusive (bone takes priority over vessel, vessel over nerve), each gets the same dilate + NN resample treatment, and they're stamped in reverse priority order so bone always wins where there's overlap.

Muscle isn't included because the Quest shader doesn't have a muscle volume layer — muscles only render via mesh, and this scan's AI coverage was too sparse to generate one.

one thing i realized, what if customers return their purchase of the add-on? would that mean they can still use the code they got when they first bought it?

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
[2026-04-24 21:21:42] ASSISTANT (Claude)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Good catch — that's a real vulnerability in the current flow. Here's the issue:

Once a user buys the IAP, gets the code + key, and activates the desktop app, the key is saved to `.regionalar_license` on their computer. If they then refund the purchase, the desktop app is already activated and keeps working forever. The license validation is entirely offline (HMAC), so there's no server to revoke it.

There are two levels of protection you could add:

**Level 1 (easy, Quest-side only):** On every Quest app launch, check `IAP.GetViewerPurchases()`. If the purchase has been refunded, hide the LICENSE panel so they can't see their key or generate a new one. This doesn't revoke an already-activated desktop, but it prevents them from activating on additional computers after refunding.

**Level 2 (full protection, requires a server):** The desktop app would need to "phone home" periodically to verify the license is still valid. This means standing up a simple server, which adds cost and complexity.

For a $9.99 add-on, Level 1 is probably the right tradeoff — the handful of people who refund after activating aren't worth the overhead of running a validation server. Meta also has refund abuse detection on their end.

Want me to implement Level 1 (hide license panel on refund)?

Good point about the master code. The Quest doesn't know about the master key — it just generates codes and keys via HMAC.

But let me verify:

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
[2026-04-24 21:23:50] ASSISTANT (Claude)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
[Tool: Read license_manager.py]

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
[2026-04-24 21:24:06] ASSISTANT (Claude)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The master key is desktop-side only and completely independent of the Quest IAP system. It bypasses all validation — `validate_key()` checks for the master key first, before any HMAC check. So the refund detection on the Quest side has zero impact on master key usage.

The refund protection is now in place:

1. **On every Quest launch**, `CheckDesktopLicensePurchase()` queries Meta's IAP API
2. **If purchase exists** → `_desktopLicenseOwned = true`, license panel shows code + key
3. **If purchase is gone (refunded)** → `_desktopLicenseOwned = false`, saved code is deleted from PlayerPrefs, license panel reverts to the purchase prompt
4. **Master key on desktop** → completely unaffected, always works regardless of Quest purchase status

This means after a refund: the user can't see or regenerate their license key on the Quest, and if they try to activate a new desktop installation they won't have a valid key. Already-activated desktops will continue working (since the `.regionalar_license` file is local), but that's an acceptable tradeoff without a server.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
[2026-04-24 22:08:46] ASSISTANT (Claude)

Now I see the problem. When the cut plane clips, the shader tries to render a cross-section slice using the raw volume texture data. At the downsampled resolution, that produces the blocky stepped voxels you're seeing. The fix is to just clip cleanly without drawing that low-res slice — let the meshes handle the visual appearance.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
[2026-04-24 22:09:35] ASSISTANT (Claude)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
[2026-04-24 22:09:44] ASSISTANT (Claude)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The problem is lines 264-280. When volume layers are on and the cut plane clips, the shader samples the raw 3D texture to draw a "slice cross-section" — but at Quest's low volume resolution, that looks like blocky voxels. The fix is to always just clip cleanly without attempting to draw that slice:

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
[2026-04-24 22:09:52] ASSISTANT (Claude)

[Tool: Edit VolumeRaymarch.shader]

[2026-04-24 22:10:02] ASSISTANT (Claude)

[2026-04-24 22:10:16] ASSISTANT (Claude)

Done. The fix is simple — instead of trying to render a cross-section slice from the low-res volume data (which produces the blocky voxel look), the shader now just clips cleanly. When the cut plane is active, everything on the clipped side is simply discarded, and the meshes (bone, vasculature, nerves, muscle) handle the visual appearance since they're smooth geometry.

Rebuild in Unity and the cut plane should clip cleanly without revealing the blocky volume underneath.

That's a classic Quest issue — world-space UI canvases lose sharpness at distance because of the texture resolution and foveated rendering. Let me check how your panel is set up:

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
[2026-04-24 22:15:13] ASSISTANT (Claude)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
[Tool: Grep 'Canvas|canvas|pixelsPerUnit|dynamicPixels|renderMode']

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
[2026-04-24 22:15:21] ASSISTANT (Claude)

[Tool: Grep 'BuildControlPanel|_ctrlCanvas.*=|renderMode|scaleFactor|dynamicPixels|referencePixels']

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
[2026-04-24 22:15:39] ASSISTANT (Claude)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The panels are using `RenderMode.WorldSpace` canvases without a `CanvasScaler`, so they render at base resolution regardless of distance. The easiest fix is to add a `CanvasScaler` with increased `dynamicPixelsPerUnit` to each canvas — this multiplies the internal render resolution so text stays sharp further away.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[2026-04-24 22:15:58] ASSISTANT (Claude)

Good, `UnityEngine.UI` is already imported (which includes `CanvasScaler`). Now I'll add a `CanvasScaler` with `dynamicPixelsPerUnit = 2.5` to each panel canvas right after it's created. This renders the canvas internally at 2.5x resolution, keeping text crisp at distance.

All five canvases now have `CanvasScaler` with `dynamicPixelsPerUnit = 2.5f`:

1. **Control panel** (tissue layers, opacity, buttons)
2. **Wi-Fi panel** (IP, download status)
3. **Library panel** (scan list)

5. **Hint panel** (onboarding text)

The `dynamicPixelsPerUnit` setting tells Unity to render the canvas text and UI elements at 2.5x the normal pixel density, so labels that looked blurry at arm's length should now be much sharper. There's a small GPU cost but it's minimal for these panel sizes on Quest.

If you want even sharper text in a future pass, the ideal solution would be to switch from Unity's built-in `Text` component to **TextMeshPro** (which uses signed distance field rendering and stays perfectly sharp at any distance), but that would be a bigger refactor. The `CanvasScaler` approach should make a noticeable improvement right away.

[2026-04-25 17:07:20] ASSISTANT (Claude)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Good news — there are a few solid options. The tricky part is licensing for a commercial app, so let me break it down by what's actually usable for you.

**Best bets for your use case:**

**Open Anatomy Project** — This is probably your best source. They have open atlases of the brain (from MRI), inner ear (from CT), knee, head & neck, and abdomen. These are high-quality, expert-curated, and designed to be freely available. You'd need to check their specific license terms for commercial use in an app.

**Visible Human Project (NIH)** — The classic full-body CT dataset from the National Library of Medicine. It's a US government work, so it's in the public domain. The resolution is excellent. You already have a head & neck volume — this could give you full torso, limbs, etc.

**Z-Anatomy** — An open-source 3D anatomy atlas based on BodyParts3D models. The .blend files are downloadable and could potentially be converted, though these are mesh-based rather than volumetric DICOM data.

**3D Slicer sample datasets** — Slicer ships with several sample volumes (brain MRI, chest CT, etc.) and their community has shared segmented anatomy atlases through the Open Anatomy project integration.

**Sources to be cautious with (academic-only licenses):**

The Cancer Imaging Archive (TCIA) and OsiriX DICOM Library both restrict to non-commercial/research use, so those wouldn't work for a paid app.

**My recommendation:** Start with the Visible Human Project since it's public domain and gives you full-body coverage, then look at Open Anatomy for region-specific atlases. You could run those DICOMs through your existing TotalSegmentator pipeline to generate the bone/muscle/vessel/nerve layers, then export as OVOL files for the Quest app.

Want me to look deeper into the licensing terms for any of these, or help set up a pipeline to batch-convert new DICOM sets into your OVOL format?

Sources:
- [Open Anatomy Project](https://www.openanatomy.org/)
- [Visible Human Project - NLM](https://www.nlm.nih.gov/research/visible/tools.html)
- [Z-Anatomy](https://lluisv.itch.io/z-anatomy)
- [3D Slicer](https://www.slicer.org/)
- [Open Access Medical Image Repositories](https://www.aylward.org/notes/open-access-medical-image-repositories)
- [Medimodel DICOM Library](https://medimodel.com/sample-dicom-files/)
- [3DICOM Library](https://3dicomviewer.com/dicom-library/)

got it, so to recap, when they purchase the license, how can they be redirected to my github for downloading the desktop app?

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
[2026-04-25 17:41:01] ASSISTANT (Claude)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
There's no automatic redirect — since this is a Quest app, you can't open a browser URL from inside the headset. Instead, here's how the flow works with what we've already built:

1. User taps the purchase button in your Quest app
2. Meta IAP completes the $9.99 transaction
3. Your app's license panel appears showing their **generated code**, the **license key**, and the **download URL** (`github.com/LaurenceHenson/RegionalAR/releases`)
4. User takes off the headset, goes to that URL on their computer, downloads and installs the desktop app
5. They enter their code + license key to activate

The download URL is displayed right on the license panel we added to `WiFiDownloader.cs`, so users can see it and type it into their computer's browser. It's a short enough URL to remember or jot down.

If you want to make it even easier, you could also add the download link to your **add-on's store description** in the Meta Developer Dashboard — that way users can see it on the store page before and after purchase from the Meta website/phone app where links are actually clickable.

# DOCX creation, editing, and analysis

## Overview

A .docx file is a ZIP archive containing XML files.

## Quick Reference

| Task | Approach |
|------|----------|
| Read/analyze content | `pandoc` or unpack for raw XML |
| Create new document | Use `docx-js` - see Creating New Documents below |
| Edit existing document | Unpack → edit XML → repack - see Editing Existing Documents below |

### Converting .doc to .docx

Legacy `.doc` files must be converted before editing:

```bash
python scripts/office/soffice.py --headless --convert-to docx document.doc
```

### Reading Content

```bash
# Text extraction with tracked changes
pandoc --track-changes=all document.docx -o output.md

# Raw XML access
python scripts/office/unpack.py document.docx unpacked/
```

### Converting to Images

```bash
python scripts/office/soffice.py --headless --convert-to pdf document.docx
pdftoppm -jpeg -r 150 document.pdf page
```

### Accepting Tracked Changes

To produce a clean document with all tracked changes accepted (requires LibreOffice):

```bash
python scripts/accept_changes.py input.docx output.docx
```

---

## Creating New Documents

Generate .docx files with JavaScript, then validate. Install: `npm install -g docx`

### Setup
```javascript
const { Document, Packer, Paragraph, TextRun, Table, TableRow, TableCell, ImageRun,
        Header, Footer, AlignmentType, PageOrientation, LevelFormat, ExternalHyperlink,
        InternalHyperlink, Bookmark, FootnoteReferenceRun, PositionalTab,
        PositionalTabAlignment, PositionalTabRelativeTo, PositionalTabLeader,
        TabStopType, TabStopPosition, Column, SectionType,
        TableOfContents, HeadingLevel, BorderStyle, WidthType, ShadingType,
        VerticalAlign, PageNumber, PageBreak } = require('docx');

const doc = new Document({ sections: [{ children: [/* content */] }] });
Packer.toBuffer(doc).then(buffer => fs.writeFileSync("doc.docx", buffer));
```

### Validation
After creating the file, validate it. If validation fails, unpack, fix the XML, and repack.
```bash
python scripts/office/validate.py doc.docx
```

### Page Size

```javascript
// CRITICAL: docx-js defaults to A4, not US Letter
// Always set page size explicitly for consistent results
sections: [{
  properties: {
    page: {
      size: {
        width: 12240,   // 8.5 inches in DXA
        height: 15840   // 11 inches in DXA
      },
      margin: { top: 1440, right: 1440, bottom: 1440, left: 1440 } // 1 inch margins
    }
  },
  children: [/* content */]
}]
```

**Common page sizes (DXA units, 1440 DXA = 1 inch):**

| Paper | Width | Height | Content Width (1" margins) |
|-------|-------|--------|---------------------------|
| US Letter | 12,240 | 15,840 | 9,360 |
| A4 (default) | 11,906 | 16,838 | 9,026 |

**Landscape orientation:** docx-js swaps width/height internally, so pass portrait dimensions and let it handle the swap:
```javascript
size: {
  width: 12240,   // Pass SHORT edge as width
  height: 15840,  // Pass LONG edge as height
  orientation: PageOrientation.LANDSCAPE  // docx-js swaps them in the XML
},
// Content width = 15840 - left margin - right margin (uses the long edge)
```

### Styles (Override Built-in Headings)

Use Arial as the default font (universally supported). Keep titles black for readability.

```javascript
const doc = new Document({
  styles: {
    default: { document: { run: { font: "Arial", size: 24 } } }, // 12pt default
    paragraphStyles: [
      // IMPORTANT: Use exact IDs to override built-in styles
      { id: "Heading1", name: "Heading 1", basedOn: "Normal", next: "Normal", quickFormat: true,
        run: { size: 32, bold: true, font: "Arial" },
        paragraph: { spacing: { before: 240, after: 240 }, outlineLevel: 0 } }, // outlineLevel required for TOC
      { id: "Heading2", name: "Heading 2", basedOn: "Normal", next: "Normal", quickFormat: true,
        run: { size: 28, bold: true, font: "Arial" },
        paragraph: { spacing: { before: 180, after: 180 }, outlineLevel: 1 } },
    ]
  },
  sections: [{
    children: [
      new Paragraph({ heading: HeadingLevel.HEADING_1, children: [new TextRun("Title")] }),
    ]
  }]
});
```

### Lists (NEVER use unicode bullets)

```javascript
// ❌ WRONG - never manually insert bullet characters
new Paragraph({ children: [new TextRun("• Item")] })  // BAD
new Paragraph({ children: [new TextRun("\u2022 Item")] })  // BAD

// ✅ CORRECT - use numbering config with LevelFormat.BULLET
const doc = new Document({
  numbering: {
    config: [
      { reference: "bullets",
        levels: [{ level: 0, format: LevelFormat.BULLET, text: "•", alignment: AlignmentType.LEFT,
          style: { paragraph: { indent: { left: 720, hanging: 360 } } } }] },
      { reference: "numbers",
        levels: [{ level: 0, format: LevelFormat.DECIMAL, text: "%1.", alignment: AlignmentType.LEFT,
          style: { paragraph: { indent: { left: 720, hanging: 360 } } } }] },
    ]
  },
  sections: [{
    children: [
      new Paragraph({ numbering: { reference: "bullets", level: 0 },
        children: [new TextRun("Bullet item")] }),
      new Paragraph({ numbering: { reference: "numbers", level: 0 },
        children: [new TextRun("Numbered item")] }),
    ]
  }]
});

// ⚠️ Each reference creates INDEPENDENT numbering
// Same reference = continues (1,2,3 then 4,5,6)
// Different reference = restarts (1,2,3 then 1,2,3)
```

### Tables

**CRITICAL: Tables need dual widths** - set both `columnWidths` on the table AND `width` on each cell. Without both, tables render incorrectly on some platforms.

```javascript
// CRITICAL: Always set table width for consistent rendering
// CRITICAL: Use ShadingType.CLEAR (not SOLID) to prevent black backgrounds
const border = { style: BorderStyle.SINGLE, size: 1, color: "CCCCCC" };
const borders = { top: border, bottom: border, left: border, right: border };

new Table({
  width: { size: 9360, type: WidthType.DXA }, // Always use DXA (percentages break in Google Docs)
  columnWidths: [4680, 4680], // Must sum to table width (DXA: 1440 = 1 inch)
  rows: [
    new TableRow({
      children: [
        new TableCell({
          borders,
          width: { size: 4680, type: WidthType.DXA }, // Also set on each cell
          shading: { fill: "D5E8F0", type: ShadingType.CLEAR }, // CLEAR not SOLID
          margins: { top: 80, bottom: 80, left: 120, right: 120 }, // Cell padding (internal, not added to width)
          children: [new Paragraph({ children: [new TextRun("Cell")] })]
        })
      ]
    })
  ]
})
```

**Table width calculation:**

Always use `WidthType.DXA` — `WidthType.PERCENTAGE` breaks in Google Docs.

```javascript
// Table width = sum of columnWidths = content width
// US Letter with 1" margins: 12240 - 2880 = 9360 DXA
width: { size: 9360, type: WidthType.DXA },
columnWidths: [7000, 2360]  // Must sum to table width
```

**Width rules:**
- **Always use `WidthType.DXA`** — never `WidthType.PERCENTAGE` (incompatible with Google Docs)
- Table width must equal the sum of `columnWidths`
- Cell `width` must match corresponding `columnWidth`
- Cell `margins` are internal padding - they reduce content area, not add to cell width
- For full-width tables: use content width (page width minus left and right margins)

### Images

```javascript
// CRITICAL: type parameter is REQUIRED
new Paragraph({
  children: [new ImageRun({
    type: "png", // Required: png, jpg, jpeg, gif, bmp, svg
    data: fs.readFileSync("image.png"),
    transformation: { width: 200, height: 150 },
    altText: { title: "Title", description: "Desc", name: "Name" } // All three required
  })]
})
```

### Page Breaks

```javascript
// CRITICAL: PageBreak must be inside a Paragraph
new Paragraph({ children: [new PageBreak()] })

// Or use pageBreakBefore
new Paragraph({ pageBreakBefore: true, children: [new TextRun("New page")] })
```

### Hyperlinks

```javascript
// External link
new Paragraph({
  children: [new ExternalHyperlink({
    children: [new TextRun({ text: "Click here", style: "Hyperlink" })],
    link: "https://example.com",
  })]
})

// Internal link (bookmark + reference)
// 1. Create bookmark at destination
new Paragraph({ heading: HeadingLevel.HEADING_1, children: [
  new Bookmark({ id: "chapter1", children: [new TextRun("Chapter 1")] }),
]})
// 2. Link to it
new Paragraph({ children: [new InternalHyperlink({
  children: [new TextRun({ text: "See Chapter 1", style: "Hyperlink" })],
  anchor: "chapter1",
})]})
```

### Footnotes

```javascript
const doc = new Document({
  footnotes: {
    1: { children: [new Paragraph("Source: Annual Report 2024")] },
    2: { children: [new Paragraph("See appendix for methodology")] },
  },
  sections: [{
    children: [new Paragraph({
      children: [
        new TextRun("Revenue grew 15%"),
        new FootnoteReferenceRun(1),
        new TextRun(" using adjusted metrics"),
        new FootnoteReferenceRun(2),
      ],
    })]
  }]
});
```

### Tab Stops

```javascript
// Right-align text on same line (e.g., date opposite a title)
new Paragraph({
  children: [
    new TextRun("Company Name"),
    new TextRun("\tJanuary 2025"),
  ],
  tabStops: [{ type: TabStopType.RIGHT, position: TabStopPosition.MAX }],
})

// Dot leader (e.g., TOC-style)
new Paragraph({
  children: [
    new TextRun("Introduction"),
    new TextRun({ children: [
      new PositionalTab({
        alignment: PositionalTabAlignment.RIGHT,
        relativeTo: PositionalTabRelativeTo.MARGIN,
        leader: PositionalTabLeader.DOT,
      }),
      "3",
    ]}),
  ],
})
```

### Multi-Column Layouts

```javascript
// Equal-width columns
sections: [{
  properties: {
    column: {
      count: 2,          // number of columns
      space: 720,        // gap between columns in DXA (720 = 0.5 inch)
      equalWidth: true,
      separate: true,    // vertical line between columns
    },
  },
  children: [/* content flows naturally across columns */]
}]

// Custom-width columns (equalWidth must be false)
sections: [{
  properties: {
    column: {
      equalWidth: false,
      children: [
        new Column({ width: 5400, space: 720 }),
        new Column({ width: 3240 }),
      ],
    },
  },
  children: [/* content */]
}]
```

Force a column break with a new section using `type: SectionType.NEXT_COLUMN`.

### Table of Contents

```javascript
// CRITICAL: Headings must use HeadingLevel ONLY - no custom styles
new TableOfContents("Table of Contents", { hyperlink: true, headingStyleRange: "1-3" })
```

### Headers/Footers

```javascript
sections: [{
  properties: {
    page: { margin: { top: 1440, right: 1440, bottom: 1440, left: 1440 } } // 1440 = 1 inch
  },
  headers: {
    default: new Header({ children: [new Paragraph({ children: [new TextRun("Header")] })] })
  },
  footers: {
    default: new Footer({ children: [new Paragraph({
      children: [new TextRun("Page "), new TextRun({ children: [PageNumber.CURRENT] })]
    })] })
  },
  children: [/* content */]
}]
```

### Critical Rules for docx-js

- **Set page size explicitly** - docx-js defaults to A4; use US Letter (12240 x 15840 DXA) for US documents
- **Landscape: pass portrait dimensions** - docx-js swaps width/height internally; pass short edge as `width`, long edge as `height`, and set `orientation: PageOrientation.LANDSCAPE`
- **Never use `\n`** - use separate Paragraph elements
- **Never use unicode bullets** - use `LevelFormat.BULLET` with numbering config
- **PageBreak must be in Paragraph** - standalone creates invalid XML
- **ImageRun requires `type`** - always specify png/jpg/etc
- **Always set table `width` with DXA** - never use `WidthType.PERCENTAGE` (breaks in Google Docs)
- **Tables need dual widths** - `columnWidths` array AND cell `width`, both must match
- **Table width = sum of columnWidths** - for DXA, ensure they add up exactly
- **Always add cell margins** - use `margins: { top: 80, bottom: 80, left: 120, right: 120 }` for readable padding
- **Use `ShadingType.CLEAR`** - never SOLID for table shading
- **Never use tables as dividers/rules** - cells have minimum height and render as empty boxes (including in headers/footers); use `border: { bottom: { style: BorderStyle.SINGLE, size: 6, color: "2E75B6", space: 1 } }` on a Paragraph instead. For two-column footers, use tab stops (see Tab Stops section), not tables
- **TOC requires HeadingLevel only** - no custom styles on heading paragraphs
- **Override built-in styles** - use exact IDs: "Heading1", "Heading2", etc.
- **Include `outlineLevel`** - required for TOC (0 for H1, 1 for H2, etc.)

---

## Editing Existing Documents

**Follow all 3 steps in order.**

### Step 1: Unpack
```bash
python scripts/office/unpack.py document.docx unpacked/
```
Extracts XML, pretty-prints, merges adjacent runs, and converts smart quotes to XML entities (`&#x201C;` etc.) so they survive editing. Use `--merge-runs false` to skip run merging.

### Step 2: Edit XML

Edit files in `unpacked/word/`. See XML Reference below for patterns.

**Use "Claude" as the author** for tracked changes and comments, unless the user explicitly requests use of a different name.

**Use the Edit tool directly for string replacement. Do not write Python scripts.** Scripts introduce unnecessary complexity. The Edit tool shows exactly what is being replaced.

**CRITICAL: Use smart quotes for new content.** When adding text with apostrophes or quotes, use XML entities to produce smart quotes:
```xml
<!-- Use these entities for professional typography -->
<w:t>Here&#x2019;s a quote: &#x201C;Hello&#x201D;</w:t>
```
| Entity | Character |
|--------|-----------|
| `&#x2018;` | ‘ (left single) |
| `&#x2019;` | ’ (right single / apostrophe) |
| `&#x201C;` | “ (left double) |
| `&#x201D;` | ” (right double) |

**Adding comments:** Use `comment.py` to handle boilerplate across multiple XML files (text must be pre-escaped XML):
```bash
python scripts/comment.py unpacked/ 0 "Comment text with &amp; and &#x2019;"
python scripts/comment.py unpacked/ 1 "Reply text" --parent 0  # reply to comment 0
python scripts/comment.py unpacked/ 0 "Text" --author "Custom Author"  # custom author name
```
Then add markers to document.xml (see Comments in XML Reference).

### Step 3: Pack
```bash
python scripts/office/pack.py unpacked/ output.docx --original document.docx
```
Validates with auto-repair, condenses XML, and creates DOCX. Use `--validate false` to skip.

**Auto-repair will fix:**
- `durableId` >= 0x7FFFFFFF (regenerates valid ID)
- Missing `xml:space="preserve"` on `<w:t>` with whitespace

**Auto-repair won't fix:**
- Malformed XML, invalid element nesting, missing relationships, schema violations

### Common Pitfalls

- **Replace entire `<w:r>` elements**: When adding tracked changes, replace the whole `<w:r>...</w:r>` block with `<w:del>...<w:ins>...` as siblings. Don't inject tracked change tags inside a run.
- **Preserve `<w:rPr>` formatting**: Copy the original run's `<w:rPr>` block into your tracked change runs to maintain bold, font size, etc.

---

## XML Reference

### Schema Compliance

- **Element order in `<w:pPr>`**: `<w:pStyle>`, `<w:numPr>`, `<w:spacing>`, `<w:ind>`, `<w:jc>`, `<w:rPr>` last
- **Whitespace**: Add `xml:space="preserve"` to `<w:t>` with leading/trailing spaces
- **RSIDs**: Must be 8-digit hex (e.g., `00AB1234`)

### Tracked Changes

**Insertion:**
```xml
<w:ins w:id="1" w:author="Claude" w:date="2025-01-01T00:00:00Z">
  <w:r><w:t>inserted text</w:t></w:r>
</w:ins>
```

**Deletion:**
```xml
<w:del w:id="2" w:author="Claude" w:date="2025-01-01T00:00:00Z">
  <w:r><w:delText>deleted text</w:delText></w:r>
</w:del>
```

**Inside `<w:del>`**: Use `<w:delText>` instead of `<w:t>`, and `<w:delInstrText>` instead of `<w:instrText>`.

**Minimal edits** - only mark what changes:
```xml
<!-- Change "30 days" to "60 days" -->
<w:r><w:t>The term is </w:t></w:r>
<w:del w:id="1" w:author="Claude" w:date="...">
  <w:r><w:delText>30</w:delText></w:r>
</w:del>
<w:ins w:id="2" w:author="Claude" w:date="...">
  <w:r><w:t>60</w:t></w:r>
</w:ins>
<w:r><w:t> days.</w:t></w:r>
```

**Deleting entire paragraphs/list items** - when removing ALL content from a paragraph, also mark the paragraph mark as deleted so it merges with the next paragraph. Add `<w:del/>` inside `<w:pPr><w:rPr>`:
```xml
<w:p>
  <w:pPr>
    <w:numPr>...</w:numPr>  <!-- list numbering if present -->
    <w:rPr>
      <w:del w:id="1" w:author="Claude" w:date="2025-01-01T00:00:00Z"/>
    </w:rPr>
  </w:pPr>
  <w:del w:id="2" w:author="Claude" w:date="2025-01-01T00:00:00Z">
    <w:r><w:delText>Entire paragraph content being deleted...</w:delText></w:r>
  </w:del>
</w:p>
```
Without the `<w:del/>` in `<w:pPr><w:rPr>`, accepting changes leaves an empty paragraph/list item.

**Rejecting another author's insertion** - nest deletion inside their insertion:
```xml
<w:ins w:author="Jane" w:id="5">
  <w:del w:author="Claude" w:id="10">
    <w:r><w:delText>their inserted text</w:delText></w:r>
  </w:del>
</w:ins>
```

**Restoring another author's deletion** - add insertion after (don't modify their deletion):
```xml
<w:del w:author="Jane" w:id="5">
  <w:r><w:delText>deleted text</w:delText></w:r>
</w:del>
<w:ins w:author="Claude" w:id="10">
  <w:r><w:t>deleted text</w:t></w:r>
</w:ins>
```

### Comments

After running `comment.py` (see Step 2), add markers to document.xml. For replies, use `--parent` flag and nest markers inside the parent's.

**CRITICAL: `<w:commentRangeStart>` and `<w:commentRangeEnd>` are siblings of `<w:r>`, never inside `<w:r>`.**

```xml
<!-- Comment markers are direct children of w:p, never inside w:r -->
<w:commentRangeStart w:id="0"/>
<w:del w:id="1" w:author="Claude" w:date="2025-01-01T00:00:00Z">
  <w:r><w:delText>deleted</w:delText></w:r>
</w:del>
<w:r><w:t> more text</w:t></w:r>
<w:commentRangeEnd w:id="0"/>
<w:r><w:rPr><w:rStyle w:val="CommentReference"/></w:rPr><w:commentReference w:id="0"/></w:r>

<!-- Comment 0 with reply 1 nested inside -->
<w:commentRangeStart w:id="0"/>
  <w:commentRangeStart w:id="1"/>
  <w:r><w:t>text</w:t></w:r>
  <w:commentRangeEnd w:id="1"/>
<w:commentRangeEnd w:id="0"/>
<w:r><w:rPr><w:rStyle w:val="CommentReference"/></w:rPr><w:commentReference w:id="0"/></w:r>
<w:r><w:rPr><w:rStyle w:val="CommentReference"/></w:rPr><w:commentReference w:id="1"/></w:r>
```

### Images

1. Add image file to `word/media/`
2. Add relationship to `word/_rels/document.xml.rels`:
```xml
<Relationship Id="rId5" Type=".../image" Target="media/image1.png"/>
```
3. Add content type to `[Content_Types].xml`:
```xml
<Default Extension="png" ContentType="image/png"/>
```
4. Reference in document.xml:
```xml
<w:drawing>
  <wp:inline>
    <wp:extent cx="914400" cy="914400"/>  <!-- EMUs: 914400 = 1 inch -->
    <a:graphic>
      <a:graphicData uri=".../picture">
        <pic:pic>
          <pic:blipFill><a:blip r:embed="rId5"/></pic:blipFill>
        </pic:pic>
      </a:graphicData>
    </a:graphic>
  </wp:inline>
</w:drawing>
```
